📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 20 Nov 2026 09:03, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:08.

Aiming to pick up where they left off before the break, Bologna will host Serie A's bottom side when Udinese visit Stadio Dall'Ara on Sunday.

After a sticky start, both clubs have already changed coaches, and the Rossoblu's newly introduced boss has sparked a surge up the standings.

Since Raffaele Palladino's arrival midway through September, Bologna have been a team transformed, winning five games from six and climbing towards the European places.

The Emilian club signed off for the international break with a run of four consecutive wins, with the highlight being a 4-2 victory over AC Milan at San Siro.

Last time out, the Rossoblu's revival continued in the Derby dell'Emilia against Parma, as their hosts were swiftly reduced to 10 men and ultimately suffered a 2-1 defeat.

So, having won none of their first five games during the short-lived Domenico Tedesco era, Bologna are now one of Serie A's form sides.

However, Palladino must still work on their awful home record, which stretches back through most of last season; so far this term, they have claimed five points from a possible 15 at the Dall'Ara.

Either home or away, Udinese have picked up just one from their last nine matches and are therefore stuck at the foot of the table.

The Bianconeri have put a meagre five points on the board so far, slumping into an unexpected crisis.

Safe mid-table finishers in back-to-back seasons under Kosta Runjaic, this campaign has completely unravelled, and even a change of coach has yet to produce results.

Just before the break, newly introduced boss Paolo Zanetti lost his first game against former club Venezia, with Udinese going down 2-1 in a crucial battle at the bottom.

Now, desperately needing some success, Zanetti must meet Palladino for the seventh time in management - to date, the pair have three wins apiece.

Unfortunately for fans of the Friulani, recent history is not on their side: they have won none of the last five meetings with Bologna, failing to even score in each of the last three.

Though Bologna will be without injured trio Jay Enem, Juan Miranda and Emil Holm, left-winger Nicolo Cambiaghi has resumed training after leaving Italy's UEFA Nations League camp.

Having impressed in the Azzurri's win over France, Cambiaghi has overcome a minor ankle problem and should start alongside Federico Bernadeschi in the final third.

The latter has previously scored four goals against Udinese, finding the net as a substitute in both of the last two meetings.

Bernardeschi and Samuel Mbangula - who recently hit a hat-trick at San Siro - are the hosts' joint-top Serie A scorers with three goals each; Jurgen Ekkelenkamp has netted three times for Udinese.

The visitors must travel without Nicolo Bertola, who has suffered a thigh injury in training and joins Idrissa Gueye on the sidelines.

In better news for Zanetti, David Alaba could return from his latest layoff, while Nicolo Zaniolo is available after withdrawing from the Italy squad for personal reasons.

Set to support Keinan Davis up front, Zaniolo has played eight league games against Bologna without ever scoring.

Bologna possible starting lineup:.

Skorupski; Darmian, Casale, Theate; Zortea, Ferguson, Pobega, Alhassane; Bernardeschi, Cambiaghi; Odgaard.

Udinese possible starting lineup:.

Okoye; Abankwah, Palma, Solet; Vojvoda, Karlstrom, Piotrowski, Kamara; Zaniolo, Ekkelenkamp; Davis.

Bologna may be in fine form but they tend to falter on home turf, while Udinese are struggling to pick up points anywhere.

Only Sassuolo have conceded more goals than the Friulani, and the Rossoblu have kept just a single clean sheet, so a score-draw could be on the cards.

Pulisic got the first goal after a brace in the previous rout, and it was an incredible overhead kick.

Pulisic was actually overlooked by Pochettino for the September-October window – partly for fitness reasons – and he spoke to reporters after the game to share his thoughts after an emotional evening. He was called the ‘best player on the pitch’ by the US media, and his words are via MilanNews.

An overhead kick goal is pretty special….

“I’ve never scored a goal like that, it was special. Weston crossed the ball and it was the only thing I could really do, so I thought I had to give it a try. It was really nice to see the ball go in.”.

Is it nice to get a victory on Pochettino’s farewell day?

“Yes, obviously he’s leaving now, so it’s nice to end with a good performance and a nice win for the team.”.

How would you describe this particular group, a mix of veterans and young players?

Barcelona vs. Villarreal: Head-to-head record and past meetings ahead of La Liga clash

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Matt Law | 20 Nov 2026 09:23, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:23.
  • Barcelona will resume their 2026-27 La Liga campaign with a home fixture against Villarreal on Sunday afternoon.
  • Hansi Flick's side are right now top of the La Liga table, boasting a record of 11 wins and one defeat from their 12 matches to collect 33 points, which has left them three points ahead of second-placed Real Madrid at this stage of proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Matt Law | 20 Nov 2026 09:23, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 09:23.

Barcelona will resume their 2026-27 La Liga campaign with a home fixture against Villarreal on Sunday afternoon.

Hansi Flick's side are right now top of the La Liga table, boasting a record of 11 wins and one defeat from their 12 matches to collect 33 points, which has left them three points ahead of second-placed Real Madrid at this stage of proceedings.

Barcelona have won their last three games in all competitions, including a 2-1 success over Atletico Madrid in their last fixture before the November international break.

Villarreal, meanwhile, have a record of four wins, three draws and five defeats from their 12 league matches this season to collect 15 points.

The Yellow Submarine are currently eighth in the division, three points behind sixth-placed Sevilla.

Here, Sports Mole looks at the head-to-head record between Barcelona and Villarreal ahead of their clash at Camp Nou this weekend.

Barcelona have tackled Villarreal on 58 occasions throughout history, and they comfortably lead the head-to-head record, posting 36 wins to Villarreal's 12, while there have also been 10 draws.

Lionel Messi is the all-time leading goalscorer in this fixture, having found the back of the net on 16 occasions against Villarreal during his time at Barcelona, while Neymar is second on nine.

As for the Yellow Submarine, former Manchester United and Atletico Madrid star Diego Forlan is their leading goalscorer against Barcelona, having netted five times against the Catalan outfit during his Villarreal career.

In La Liga, there have been 52 meetings, with Barcelona's winning 32 times to Villarreal's 11, while the points have been shared on nine occasions in Spain's top flight.

Villarreal incredibly recorded a 5-3 victory away to Barcelona in January 2024 and 3-2 win in May 2025, either side of a 5-1 triumph for the Catalan team in September 2024.

However, they were most recently downed 2-0 by La Blaugrana at Estadio de la Ceramica in December 2025, with centre-back Renato Veiga being sent off for a reckless tackle on Lamine Yamal, who went on to score the second for Hansi Flick's side.

Villarreal's last three wins over Barcelona have all come away from home, and they have not actually managed to beat the Catalan side in front of their own supporters since October 2007.

Barcelona's dominance in this fixture is perhaps best highlighted by the fact that they have won 12 of the last 15 La Liga meetings between the two clubs, even if Villarreal have enjoyed strong spells such as when they recorded three straight victories between April 2007 and March 2008.

The last meeting between the two sides took place at Camp Nou in February 2026, with Barcelona recording a 4-1 win.

Barcelona will now be looking to post a third straight victory over Villarreal.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 08:14 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 10:33 EST, 19 November 2026.

Manchester United have released their latest financial results after spending another £15million to install Mauricio Pochettino as the club’s newly introduced head coach.

United’s first quarter financials up to September 30 don’t include the cost of paying the US Soccer Federation £10m to buy Pochettino and his backroom staff out of their contracts, or an additional £5m to pay off Michael Carrick and his staff.

They show that United brought in total revenues of £146.1m compared to £140.3m in the first quarter last year, but made an operating loss for the quarter of £3m compared with an operating profit of £13m 12 months ago.

The results come just weeks after co-owner Avram Glazer told a conference that the club’s value is not dependent on success on the pitch.

Sources say that United acted early in the season to address the drop in form under Carrick that saw United slide into the relegation zone, and the club are now focused on improving results under Pochettino.

The Argentine is expected to be given a modest transfer budget in January to make new signings, with United in the market for a striker, left-back and centre-back.

Man United's latest financial results come after the Glazers said that success isn't dependent on results.

The results don't include the £10m United paid to buy Pochettino and his staff from the US national team.

Chief executive Omar Berrada mentioned: ‘Our revenue remains strong and on track, while we continue to grow sustainably. We are pleased to welcome Mauricio Pochettino and his staff to the club and our priority is to support them as we look continuously to improve our performances on the pitch.’.

According to recent reports, the latest results only cover the first five Premier League fixtures of the season, one Champions League match and the League Cup defeat to Brighton. Sources insist that they show the benefit of the cost-cutting under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos and what they say is improved operational efficiency.

United have reiterated their guidance of total revenues of £740-£760m for this financial year after reporting that the first quarter saw rises in broadcast (£5.3m), retail (£1.3m) and matchday (£0.6m) revenues.

However, sponsorship revenue was down by £1.4m despite a upcoming training kit deal with Betway, largely due to United playing individual pre-season friendlies rather than going on summer tour.

Employee benefit expenses for the quarter were £79.9m, an increase of £6.3m due mainly to players' wages going up 25 per cent after qualifying for the Champions League.

United's borrowing has increased 19 per cent from a year ago, with the club's historic US dollar debt up $125m to $775m 'as a result of the refinancing of our senior secured notes in June 2026'.

In a recent development, this rise, which was revealed in the last set of results in September, equates to £577.4m, up from £481.2m. The net cost of financing that debt dropped from £21.4m to £14.5m.

Meanwhile, United’s borrowing on the club's revolving credit facility was £207.1m as of September 30, down from £268m a year ago.

  • Saka's injury occurred in the first half of Arsenal's 2-2 draw with the Bundesliga champions on October 21, and Arteta immediately conceded at full time that the winger's problem looked severe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 10:00.

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta has revealed that Bukayo Saka will spend another four weeks on the sidelines with the quadriceps injury he sustained against Bayern Munich in the Champions League.

Saka's injury occurred in the first half of Arsenal's 2-2 draw with the Bundesliga champions on October 21, and Arteta immediately conceded at full time that the winger's problem looked severe.

Reports emerging soon after stated that Saka would miss between six and eight weeks, although Arsenal have been loath to put an exact timeframe on the Englishman's recovery just yet.

However, speaking to the media ahead of Saturday's Premier League clash with Newcastle United, Arteta admitted that Saka was only halfway into his recovery process and would spend the full eight weeks out.

It has been revealed that "We had another test. It looks like it’s going to be an eight week injury more or less. He’s four weeks in now," the Spaniard told reporters.

Saka missing another four weeks means that the 25-year-old is set to sit out another seven matches across all competitions, including a number of heavyweight fixtures.

Arsenal host Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League next Tuesday, before ending the month with a clash of the titans against Manchester City in the Premier League.

Saka is also expected to miss matches with Brentford, Tottenham Hotspur and Real Madrid in early December, and he will most likely be unavailable for the visit of Bournemouth on December 13 too.

However, the attacker could be fit to make his comeback against Mauricio Pochettino's Manchester United on December 20, until when Noni Madueke and Max Dowman will provide cover.

Dowman will serve the third of his three-game domestic suspension against Newcastle this weekend, but Madueke has earned numerous plaudits in recent weeks, having scored against Slavia Prague in the Champions League before firing the effort that led to Martin Odegaard's winner against Hull City.

Saka will likely be one of two core members of Arsenal's title-winning team to miss matches against Tottenham and Real Madrid, as Arteta also delivered negative news on Martin Zubimendi.

The midfielder appeared to hurt his hamstring in Spain's 3-2 Nations League defeat to England during the international break, and he also faces around a month on the sidelines.

Sources indicate that "He has a problem in his hamstring. The scan shows there is an injury there he will be out for a few weeks," Arteta added on Zubimendi.

However, the 27-year-old is yet to start a Premier League game this season and was always expected to lose out to Declan Rice and Bruno Guimaraes at St James' Park tomorrow.

Arsenal are five points clear at the top of the Premier League table heading into gameweek 11 and are searching for their fourth successive win over Newcastle in the top flight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered.
  • How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just when the Premier League and the world outside of east Manchester and Abu Dhabi needed Liverpool to step up, to strike back, to make a point, they faltered. Maybe it was unfair to expect them to do so, given the circumstances. But unfairness, lack of clarity and uncertainty are all prevailing moods in English football at present.

How we had rubbed our hands in anticipation of Manchester City having to play their first league fixture here at Anfield after being found guilty of industrial-scale fraud with 114 of the 115 financial charges being proven against them.

Industry observers note that it felt apt that it was at the home of Liverpool, who, along with Arsenal, possess the strongest sense of grievance at having been denied trophies and glory by City’s cheating. As expected, there were banners everywhere at Anfield. “A generation of supporters cheated,” one read and it summed up the depth of the anger.

Their fans would surely create the kind of bear-pit atmosphere that would leave City in no doubt at the vitriol that will rain down on them from now on. At every away ground. Liverpool could set the tone. The defiance.

This is a team who can stir the blood, surf the emotion and triumph against the odds more than any other; who have a proud history of doing so. Who feel the injustice at its most acute and could feed off that.

In the end Liverpool suffered their first defeat of the season. Their first under Andoni Iraola. And comprehensively so. It could not have come at a worse time for them and for the Premier League, and for the fans of every other club who wanted to see City humbled. On the pitch.

In a recent development, there was another sense of injustice. Up until the dismissal of Ryan Gravenberch, Liverpool were the better side. Especially as they attacked the Kop in the second half, drawing saves from Gianluigi Donnarumma, and began to build the kind of momentum that has, over the years, appeared to suck the ball into the net.

Ryan Gravenberch is OFF 🟥 https://t.co/IVIHNzqw6k.

According to recent reports, the midfielder’s first yellow card looked harsh. His second, for a foul on substitute Jérémy Doku was less so (but still not clear-cut) and it meant Liverpool had to play the final third of the game with 10 men. Instead of weaponising that; they wilted and the fans directed their frustration at referee Chris Kavanagh, believing he was lenient towards City.

It has been revealed that this is not a slight on Iraola, but it is hard to imagine Jürgen Klopp not riding that wave of emotion more effectively and wringing more out of the available players. Turning to the fans; imploring them; cajoling them.

According to recent reports, instead it was City making the statement with an extraordinary power play as they scored three times in 13 minutes, inspired by Doku, whose cameo made him man of the match. That City could hold the winger back, on the bench, only to introduce him with such devastating effect again pointed to their phenomenal strength in depth.

Industry observers note that they are again three points clear at the top, with six wins from six games, ahead of champions Arsenal and there is a frightening awesomeness about them at present that will make the Premier League shudder. For several reasons. What if they run away with it this season before being sanctioned, probably sometime in the spring? Where will that leave the competition?

Recent findings suggest that in the face of City’s power and the adversity of losing Gravenberch, Liverpool simply could not cope. They were already depleted – without Dominik Szoboszlai, Alexander Isak, Hugo Ekitike and Cody Gakpo – and needed some of their other massive signings to respond.

Recent findings suggest that but this was not a good day for Bradley Barcola or Florian Wirtz, in particular, and it felt telling that the latter was withdrawn soon after Erling Haaland opened the scoring. He could, in fact, have also been sent off after catching Elliot Anderson late. The German’s contribution was once more woefully negligible; worryingly marginal. He was lightweight and so, ultimately, were Liverpool.

Erling Haaland gives Manchester City the lead against Liverpool 🎯 https://t.co/cELo5y60Fk.

In fact, Liverpool’s best performers were the young attackers Victor Muñoz and, making his first league start as a makeshift centre-forward, Lewis Koumas, who is just 21. Against that, City unleashed a battery of forward talent.

"Koumas & Munoz were better than the two £100million players!" Jamie Carragher is still disappointed with what he's seeing from Florian Wirtz in a Liverpool shirt 😬🔴 https://t.co/jJwOZbPJ4b.

It has been revealed that was it an unfair advantage? It appears City have been thriving off that for some time and, while this team were not signed during the years the club have been found guilty of cheating, the argument is, of course, that they would not have joined without the sporting supremacy.

According to recent reports, certainly not Haaland, despite his avowed love for City. That cannot be doubted as his father, Alf-Inge, a former midfielder for the club, stood celebrating in the away end. The striker missed one chance when he should have scored, sent through on goal, shaking his head in disbelief at getting his angles wrong. It felt like a warning and that went unheeded as Doku, who had replaced one of their big summer signings in Iliman Ndiaye, cut in from the left with his shot deflecting into Haaland’s path. He made no mistake with a powerful, first-time finish.

Doku soon added a second, a sublime strike, as he dribbled goalwards, defenders backing off, and he arced a right-footed shot high beyond Alisson Becker’s grasp.

"It's a GEM" 💎 A beautiful strike from Jérémy Doku to double Man City's lead! https://t.co/lCUFfQmdLC.

It has been revealed that there were delighted chants of “olé” from the City supporters and that arrogance was rewarded by a strutting, emphatic third goal. It was finished by the mercurial Rayan Cherki after he was sent clear by a backheel from Josko Gvardiol, another substitute.

A moment of individual brilliance from Rayan Cherki to put the game beyond all doubt 🤯 https://t.co/wvmTMZcGhW.

It captured City’s swagger, their sense of responding to what they regard as an injustice – that they maintain will be overturned on appeal – the sense they are going to continue to create an almighty headache for the Premier League. In a sea of uncertainty as to what will now happen, that is something we can be sure of.

It has been revealed that “Cheats,” loudly boomed around Anfield from the home fans before the PA played Fleetwood Mac’s Tell Me Lies at the final whistle, as the players walked off. Those signs of defiance were not matched on the pitch. Although it may be a song City will get used to hearing for the rest of this extraordinary, unprecedented campaign.

Enzo Maresca hailed Manchester City’s ability to “make our own noise” after their emphatic 3-0 win at Liverpool.

In the first fixture since being found guilty of all but one of the 115 charges laid against them for serious breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, City made their statement on the pitch as they re-established a three-point lead at the top of the table.

“It was not easy for the players after the last two, three weeks, but they dealt with it very well,” Maresca, the head coach, said. “I said during the week we need to learn to deal with the outside noise because of the situation, because that will be there. But we have to make our own noise.

Sources indicate that “Zero-three at Anfield away is a great result, for sure. I think all the organisation needs a win like this. It’s good for all [of] the club.”.

Maresca said City will have to get used to such hostile occasions, with Liverpool fans making clear their anger over the judgment, and added: “All the away games are going to be with noise.”.

Maresca confirmed that chief executive Ferran Soriano and director of football Hugo Viana had travelled on the team bus to Anfield in a sign of unity.

“Ferran was there, Hugo was there. We were all together,” Maresca said. “For the importance of the game, Liverpool away, Anfield away. It’s good to be together.”.

The Italian claimed that despite the verdict, and the attention and uncertainty as to what will happen next, it had not affected his squad.

“The players just focus on the football. They are not thinking about the future,” he said. “It’s how we learn to deal with the noise. It’s our duty to make noise and to do that we win games. You cannot imagine how happy I am. Hopefully I am going to speak about this situation when we are going to win the appeal.”.

The Liverpool boss told BBC MOTD: “I think the first part is that we played two different games. One until the red card, and then after. For 60 minutes, the players were very good. The second game from the red card was where City were better than us.

It has been revealed that “The first yellow card was just a kick in the toe. It was nothing. It was a normal foul. It was the moment when we were pushing more. The momentum was coming for us and the atmosphere in the stadium was so nice. We conceded very little in the first half. We did a really good job. The second half, we were translating into chances.

In a recent development, “You learn a lot in games like today. I am very proud of my players. They put the work rate and everything in today. It’s a loss and we didn’t get anything from the performance but I liked it a lot.”.

“The international break is good because we can review what we have done and what we can do better,” Enzo Maresca stated after Manchester City’s harum-scarum 5-3 victory over Sunderland. “But at the same time we can relax a little bit more.” One wonders how much respite Enzo Maresca and Manchester City actually enjoyed in the intervening 21 days.

Since City last kicked a football in anger, they have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled at them by the Premier League in a verdict that has shaken professional football to its very core. The club have appealed and the extent of their punishment now rests with an independent panel. Until then, though, the show goes on and City’s players and staff must compete knowing that their every move now comes with a caveat.

It has been revealed that city have put up a united front and on Thursday Maresca and Haaland duly delivered the party lines, the City head coach revealing that the feeling among his charges was “fantastic”. “[My players] know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things,” Maresca mentioned, before adding that he trusts the club “completely”. The Italian doubled down on his remarks in his Friday press conference.

City maintain their innocence and many of Maresca’s peers have remained tight-lipped on the case, though Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick admitted this week he has questions, while Régis Le Bris urged football’s governing bodies to be “relentless” in safeguarding competitive integrity.

Given all that has happened, it would be easy to forget that this is, for now, a top-of-the-table clash and has been one of the Premier League’s marquee rivalries since the days of Guardiola-Jürgen Klopp. Liverpool fans have never been ones to roll out the red carpet when City are in town, but the ill feeling and belligerence will only intensify at Anfield this time around owing to the events of the past weeks.

City are top of the league having won all five of their league matches so far, while Liverpool have huffed and puffed to sixth, remaining unbeaten.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 20 Nov 2026 10:04.

Burnley play host to rivals Blackburn Rovers looking for the win that would ensure that they avoid being cut adrift in the relegation zone.

At a time when the Clarets sit in 22nd position in the Championship table, Rovers return after the international break in 13th place.

When Burnley stormed into a 4-1 lead at Cardiff City earlier this month, Fabio Celestini would have been confident that he was recording his first win as head coach that would also kick-start the club's season.

Instead, a 29-minute capitulation that resulted in a 5-4 defeat in South Wales has left relegation feeling increasingly likely, even though the season is only just under a third of the way complete.

Burnley remain on 10 points from 15 matches, their only success coming at fellow strugglers Watford, and they are already five points adrift of safety.

Although an upturn in fortunes would see them promptly haul themselves back into contention to avoid the drop, conceding 31 goals - the worst defensive record in the Championship - will not fill supporters with confidence.

Five of Burnley's seven Championship games at Turf Moor this season have ended in draws, but they remain the only team in the division without a home victory.

As for Blackburn, they have an interim management team in place after Tony Mowbray stood down from his position earlier this week due to health issues.

Rovers sit 11 points above their fierce rivals in the standings, the pre-season expectation having been that the points difference would be close to the exact opposite at this stage of the campaign.

Nevertheless, Blackburn have won five of their last nine fixtures in the second tier to keep them in the hunt for a playoff spot.

The 2-1 victory over West Ham United in their last outing made it five wins from eight matches at Ewood Park.

However, Rovers have prevailed in just one of their seven away fixtures, a 1-0 success at Bristol City on October 13.

Blackburn Rovers Championship form:.

Celestini will inevitably make changes to his Burnley XI, with Max Alleyne and Josh Cullen among those who could return in defence and midfield.

Goalkeeper Max Weiss may potentially be handed a recall between the sticks in place of Gregoire Coubert, while Zeki Amdouni could start on the left flank.

However, Connor Roberts starts a three-game ban, a consequence of an incident at the end of the Cardiff game that led to retrospective punishment.

Despite Damien Johnson and Mike Dodds taking the reins from Mowbray, the Blackburn XI will look similar from the victory over West Ham.

However, second-choice goalkeeper Aynsley Pears is expected to deputise for Balazs Toth, who suffered a finger injury while on international duty with Hungary.

If the likes of Mathias Jorgensen and Ryoya Morishita overcome injuries in time for this fixture, they will likely be named on the substitutes' bench at best.

Burnley possible starting lineup:.

Weiss; Walker, Ekdal, Alleyne, Pires; Hatate, Cullen; Ramazani, Edwards, Amdouni; Hountondji.

Blackburn Rovers possible starting lineup:.

Pears; Beyuku, Carter, McLoughlin, Pickering; Morsy, Montgomery; Fevrier, Cantwell, Afolayan; Gudjohnsen.

With Burnley struggling for wins and Blackburn having to adapt with Mowbray in charge, this points to a game where both teams would be happy to avoid a defeat. Therefore, we anticipate a low-scoring draw being played out at Turf Moor.

#72547. Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 94m • 📚 Deep Dive (18750 w)

Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 94 min read (18750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~94 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2.
  • Recent findings suggest that alzheimer’s disease (AD) is an age-associated neurodegenerative disease affecting millions worldwide, with a prevalence of roughly 10–30% among individuals older than 65 years3.
  • It has been revealed that the hypothalamus, a small but complex brain region, orchestrates a wide range of physiological and neuroendocrine processes frequently dysregulated in ageing and AD2,7.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions revealed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand–receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

Recent findings suggest that alzheimer’s disease (AD) is an age-associated neurodegenerative disease affecting millions worldwide, with a prevalence of roughly 10–30% among individuals older than 65 years3. Although its cardinal feature is cognitive impairment, AD manifests as a systemic condition involving profound disruptions in sleep, circadian rhythms, metabolic homeostasis, stress responses and neuroendocrine functions1. The canonical neuropathological hallmarks are extracellular amyloid-β plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), which alongside widespread neuroinflammation and volumetric brain changes, also intensify with ageing1,4. Because cognitive decline has traditionally guided both diagnosis and research, investigation has focused mainly on the hippocampus and cortex5. As the effects of AD on other brain regions remain poorly understood, investigating these understudied areas is crucial for elucidating the full spectrum of disease mechanisms and developing upcoming therapeutics6.

It has been revealed that the hypothalamus, a small but complex brain region, orchestrates a wide range of physiological and neuroendocrine processes frequently dysregulated in ageing and AD2,7. Emerging evidence suggests that hypothalamic dysfunction not only correlates with but also actively exacerbates AD pathology and cognitive decline1. Specifically, pathology within hypothalamic subregions, such as the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)8, arcuate nucleus (ARC)1,9 and mammillary body10, has been associated with prominent sleep disturbances, metabolic dysfunction and memory deficits observed in patients with AD. These systemic disruptions, in turn, are proposed to create a vicious cycle that further accelerates disease progression and cognitive decline1.

Industry observers note that despite its central role in homeostasis and brain ageing2,11, the hypothalamus remains an understudied region in the context of human ageing and AD. In particular, we have a limited understanding of the volumetric, cellular and molecular changes within the human hypothalamus during these processes. Although studies in animal models have highlighted hypothalamic involvement in ageing and neurodegeneration2,11,12, human studies remain scarce. This may be in part because the hypothalamus is more evolutionarily conserved than the cortex and is critical for survival, and thus it may show less overt vulnerability to ageing and prevalent diseases13. This paucity is especially pronounced for investigations that combine high-resolution imaging with single-cell analyses, complementary approaches essential for dissecting the anatomical and cellular heterogeneity of this complex brain region. This knowledge gap hinders our ability to determine how specific hypothalamic subregions and cell populations contribute to ageing and AD, and why they show differential vulnerability.

According to recent reports, here we present HypoAD, a multimodal atlas combining two powerful, cross-scale approaches. First, we performed high-resolution volumetric analysis of clinical imaging data from 458 individuals across the adult lifespan with varying cognitive and amyloid-β pathological statuses. Second, we generated a complementary single-cell transcriptomic atlas, comprising 614,403 nuclei from the hypothalami of 17 post-mortem donors, including young and older individuals with or without clinical and neuropathological diagnoses of AD, in which sampling was specifically enriched for the SCN, ARC and mammillary body. This dual-modality approach reveals the subregion-specific and cell-type-specific alterations of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD.

It has been revealed that neuroimaging studies have reported changes in hypothalamic volumes associated with ageing and cognitive decline14. Previous analyses were low-resolution or limited to major areas, masking disease-relevant subregions such as the ARC and SCN14. To overcome this limitation, we leveraged a newly developed volumetric atlas of the human hypothalamus15 to delineate and measure 13 hypothalamic and 12 extrahypothalamic structures (Supplementary Table 1). Our analysis included a clinical imaging dataset of 458 individuals across two previously described cohorts: the Adult Metabolism & Brain Resilience (AMBR) study16 (n = 202) and the Connectomics in Brain Aging and Dementia (CBA) study17 (n = 256) (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

Sources indicate that pearson correlation analysis revealed that whereas total hypothalamic volume revealed a weak correlation with age (r = 0.15, adjusted P = 1.5 × 10 −3, Fig. 1a, Supplementary Table 2), its constituent subregions showed stronger age-related correlations. Specifically, the lateral hypothalamus volume was negatively correlated with age (r = −0.22, adjusted P = 5.2 × 10−6), suggesting age-related atrophy. By contrast, the volumes of the SCN (r = 0.26, adjusted P = 2.8 × 10−8), ARC (r = 0.32, adjusted P = 1.7 × 10−11), paraventricular nucleus (r = 0.35, adjusted P = 6.9 × 10−14), periventricular nucleus (r = 0.34, adjusted P = 8.8 × 10−13) and dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH) (r = 0.23, adjusted P = 1.8 × 10−6) all increased with age across all 458 individuals in two studies: AMBR and CBA (Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). A few subregions (SCN, mammillary body, dorsal periventricular nucleus and tuberomammillary nucleus) showed lower test–retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) < 0.4; Extended Data Fig. 1b), probably reflecting their small size and limited tissue contrast; volumetric results for these subregions should therefore be interpreted with caution. In the AMBR cohort the positive correlation between DMH volume and age was not detected in cognitively normal, amyloid-β negative individuals (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3), but it remained present in the larger harmonized two-study cohort (n = 458; Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). To test whether this age-related increase in DMH volume itself differs by disease status, an age × group interaction model (group: cognitively normal and amyloid-negative versus all others; Methods) showed no significant interaction (effect size/estimate ± standard error (s.e.) = −0.041 ± 0.025, adjusted P = 0.12, Supplementary Table 4), indicating that age-related increase in DMH volume does not differ significantly between groups. This suggests that the DM–age association probably reflects a general feature of hypothalamic ageing in this subregion—which is implicated in sleep–wakefulness18 and body-weight regulation19—rather than a process specific to neurodegeneration.

a, Pearson correlation heatmap of subregion volumes and age at MRI. Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Boxes mark five clusters (complete linkage on 1 − r). All subregions were analysed. Benjamini–Hochberg correction covers unique pairwise correlations (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). b, Age–volume Pearson r in pooled (black, n = 458), CBA (orange, n = 256) and AMBR (blue, n = 202) analyses. n denotes independent participants. Filled circles indicate Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P < 0.05 across 26 correlations per analysis. Open circles indicate non-significance. Two-sided Pearson tests in a,b. c, Age (left) and female-sex (right, male reference) effects from Gaussian identity-link models of log-volume, adjusting for age, sex, cognitive and amyloid-β status, their interaction, ICV and study (n = 316 independent participants with complete covariate data, 197 female, 119 male, CBA 209, AMBR 107). Points show coefficients. Bars show unadjusted 95% confidence intervals (estimate ±1.96 × s.e.). Age effects are per 11.61 years (full-cohort s.d.). Two-sided t-tests use 308 residual degrees of freedom, with Benjamini–Hochberg correction across eight coefficients, including the intercept, per model. Colours indicate adjusted P. Supplementary Table 4 supplies estimates, intervals, t statistics and raw and adjusted P. d, Three-dimensional MRI reconstructions from three representative women. e, PCA of raw subregion volumes, coloured by age, sex, amyloid-β and cognitive status on PC1 and PC2. Each point represents one participant. f, Female age–volume scatter plots of selected subregions and the total hypothalamus (mm3, n = 277 independent participants), coloured by cognitive and/or amyloid-β status. Each point represents one participant. Black LOESS curves estimate conditional means. Shading shows pointwise 95% confidence intervals. AHA, anterior hypothalamic area; DPEH, dorsal periventricular nucleus; HYPO, hypothalamus; LH, lateral hypothalamus; MM, mammillary body; MPO, medial preoptic nucleus; NS, not significant; Pa, paraventricular nucleus; Pe, periventricular nucleus; PH, posterior hypothalamus; s.d., standard deviation; SO, supraoptic nucleus; TM, tuberomammillary nucleus; VM, ventromedial nucleus.

In a generalized linear model (GLM) controlling for biological sex, intracranial volume (ICV), cognitive status and amyloid-β pathology, lateral hypothalamus volume decreased with age (effect size/estimate ± s.e. = −0.021 ± 0.0064, adjusted P = 0.0019). The SCN (0.059 ± 0.018, adjusted P = 0.0029), ARC (0.058 ± 0.012, adjusted P = 4.2 × 10−6), paraventricular nucleus (0.14 ± 0.019, adjusted P = 1.8 × 10−11), periventricular nucleus (0.092 ± 0.019, adjusted P = 6.4 × 10−6), DMH (0.055 ± 0.016, adjusted P = 0.0011) and total hypothalamic volumes (0.022 ± 0.0071, adjusted P = 0.0048) showed a positive association with age (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4). Biological sex was also a significant factor: females showed smaller volumes in several subregions, most prominently in the supraoptic nucleus (−0.097 ± 0.019, adjusted P = 1.7 × 10−6) (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4). This aligns with previous studies emphasizing the sexually dimorphic nature of the hypothalamus, including the supraoptic nucleus2,14. As expected, most subregion volumes were positively correlated with ICV (Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4). For comparison, volumes of most extrahypothalamic structures showed age-related reductions, smaller sex differences than the hypothalamus and positive correlations with ICV (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 4). Representative subregions were reconstructed in three dimensions (Fig. 1d).

To holistically evaluate volumetric relationships, we performed principal component analysis (PCA) on volumetric data from all 25 delineated hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structures (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). The first two principal components (PCs) were primarily associated with age, sex and global scaling factors (intracranial and total brain volume), along which individuals separated (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Amyloid-β and cognitive status highlighted weaker associations with these components, and after residualizing for age, sex and global scaling factors, neither remained significantly associated with the leading PCs (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). This indicates that disease status does not define an independent dominant axis of macrostructural variation, and that the more sensitive disease-associated signal may instead be captured at the molecular level.

In a recent development, examination of volumetric trajectories by means of scatter plots stratified by cognitive and amyloid-β status revealed subregion-specific patterns that also differed by sex (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Notably, individuals with AD (defined as cognitive decline and amyloid-β positivity) revealed reduced total hypothalamus and lateral hypothalamus volumes compared with their age-matched non-AD counterparts, consistent with the overall age-related decline of these regions (Extended Data Fig. 3g). By contrast, ARC, SCN, paraventricular nucleus, periventricular nucleus and DMH volumes were increased in individuals with AD relative to age-matched non-AD individuals (Extended Data Fig. 3g). This pattern did not reach statistical significance, potentially reflecting the insensitivity of volumetric measures to the relatively early disease stage and the limited sample size (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Subregion volumes classified cognitive status, amyloid-β status and AD better than total hypothalamic volume (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), suggesting that subregion-specific volumetric changes capture disease-relevant variation that is obscured when the hypothalamus is treated as a single structure.

Thus, ageing is associated with subregion-specific volumetric changes that persist after controlling for amyloid-β and cognition, whereas AD-linked changes did not reach significance, motivating a complementary, higher-resolution molecular modality.

It has been revealed that volumetric data provide anatomical context but cannot reveal cell-type-specific molecular changes. We therefore performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on post-mortem hemi-hypothalamus tissue from 14 individuals (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 4a): seven with mostly early-stage AD (n = 6 sporadic, n = 1 familial) and seven age-matched, cognitively and neuropathologically normal control participants. The familial AD sample (AD_44, ID 7A in Fig. 2b; APOE4/4) was excluded from all differential analyses and retained as an extreme example of advanced pathology.

Industry observers note that a, Schematic of the snRNA-seq workflow. Frozen post-mortem hypothalamic tissue from 14 individuals (7 non-AD control participants and 7 patients with AD (6 age-matched sporadic and 1 younger familial)) was macrodissected to enrich for the ARC, SCN and mammillary nucleus (MN) subregions. Nuclei were isolated, and libraries were prepared and sequenced on a NovaSeq platform. The resulting data were integrated with 133,879 publicly available nuclei from three young, healthy control participants, yielding a final dataset of 614,403 nuclei across young control, older control (non-AD) and AD groups for comparative analysis. b, Overview of the 14 individuals included in the snRNA-seq study, detailing sample IDs, clinical condition (non-AD control, early-stage AD or familial AD), age at death and Braak stage. Each individual contributed tissue from three hypothalamic subregions (ARC, SCN and MN), totalling 42 tissue samples processed across seven experimental batches. c, UMAP plot of the integrated 614,403 nuclei. Distinct clusters represent identified main cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, ependymal cells, fibroblasts, epithelial cells, OPCs and leukocytes. Each cell type is annotated and highlighted with a unique colour. d, Dot plot of selected marker genes. Dot size corresponds to the fraction of cells within a given cell type expressing the marker; colour intensity indicates the average normalized expression level. e, Normalized expression of key canonical marker genes mapped onto the UMAP plot from c. Representative markers include GFAP (astrocytes), FLT1 (endothelial cells), CFAP299 (ependymal cells), TTR (epithelial cells), C1QA (microglia), PTPRC/CD45 (leukocytes), SYT1 (neurons), MBP (oligodendrocytes), VCAN (OPCs) and COL1A1 (fibroblasts). Illustrations in a created in BioRender; Yu, D. https://biorender.com/zt57wnj (2026).

It has been revealed that donors with AD predominantly had sporadic, clinically confirmed cognitive decline with pathology (Braak stage IV; Fig. 2b), a stage optimal for detecting transcriptional changes while neuronal populations remain20. Hierarchical clustering grouped samples by pathology status rather than by confounders such as time of death or quality metrics (Extended Data Fig. 4a).

Recent findings suggest that for annotation, we integrated our dataset with 133,879 previously published, high-quality human hypothalamic nuclei from three younger individuals (29, 42 and 50 years of age)21,22 using the single-cell variational inference algorithm23. Main cell types were identified through the expression of canonical marker genes (Fig. 2c–e and quality control in Extended Data Fig. 4b–g).

Industry observers note that to identify transcriptomic features distinguishing hypothalamic cells from patients with AD versus control individuals, we trained Elastic Net models on 36,600 genes from 480,524 cells. The dataset spanned seven independent batches, each containing one donor with AD and one control donor (Fig. 3a). This balanced design enabled a leave-one-batch-out cross-validation that yielded strong classification performance for both the all-cell model and cell-type-specific models for the main cell types (Fig. 3b).

Recent findings suggest that averaging absolute gene weights across the seven outer cross-validation folds gave the top 20 features per classifier (Fig. 3c), many previously implicated in AD pathology, lending biological support to our model’s predictions. The all-cell model’s top features included arginine–vasopressin (encoded by AVP), a circadian neuropeptide elevated in AD24. Cell-type-specific models likewise highlighted AD-linked genes: MCF2L (differentially methylated in AD; oligodendrocyte)25, ARL17B (an inhibitory neuron expression quantitative trait locus elevated in AD cortex; neurons)26, CHI3L1 (astrocyte-secreted neuroinflammation marker and a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarker for early AD diagnosis; astrocytes)27, RNF150 (a cis-expression quantitative trait locus, microglia)28 and ITGA8 (linked to demyelination; oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC))29 (Fig. 3c).

Ranking genes by mean rank across the five most abundant cell types identified HP1BP3 as the top shared feature (Fig. 3d), a candidate modulator of hippocampal cognitive ageing affected by metformin30,31 but underexplored in the hypothalamus. A per-gene specificity rank (Fig. 3e) revealed strong enrichment of long noncoding RNAs (for example, LINC02646, LINC00551, LINC01250, LINC00937 and LINC02389) among top neuronal features (Fig. 3e), providing a cell-type-specific resource of known and new AD-associated genes. Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on the ranked predictive genes revealed a significant enrichment for circadian rhythm and inflammatory pathways (Fig. 3f, Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 5), connecting our cell-level classifiers to established hallmarks of neurodegeneration.

We next performed pseudobulk differential expression analysis (edgeR likelihood-ratio test (LRT), by cell type and sample) between early-AD and control samples (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 6). Notably, microglia indicated the largest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), highlighting their substantial transcriptional response even in early AD.

For orthogonal validation, we leveraged a human CSF proteome dataset from healthy control participants and individuals with AD. Among the significantly differentially abundant proteins (Supplementary Table 7), five corresponded to significant DEGs across main cell types, three in endothelial cells, a primary component of the blood–brain barrier (Extended Data Fig. 6a): increased hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT) and decreased brain-derived neurotrophic factor and neuropeptide Y. These align with blood–brain barrier dysfunction as an early AD feature32, reduced brain-derived neurotrophic factor and neuropeptide Y reflecting loss of neuroprotection33,34 and elevated HPRT suggesting the purine-salvage stress response35. Microglial PGK1 upregulation indicates a glycolytic shift characteristic of pro-inflammatory microglia36,37. PTPRN points to an altered OPC state38. GSEA on microglial DEGs revealed enrichment for G2M checkpoint, mTORC1 signalling and cholesterol homeostasis. These findings suggest that in early AD, microglia may enter a complex, supportive state. The mTORC1 signature points to metabolic reprogramming, and the cholesterol homeostasis signature is consistent with enhanced cholesterol efflux linked to amyloid-β phagocytosis, together suggesting an early supportive microglial response (Fig. 4b).

It has been revealed that because cellular senescence contributes to ageing and neurodegeneration39, we scored three senescence signatures—Canonical senescence, Senescence responses and Senescence initiators (Fig. 4c)—alongside three overlapping NFT signatures39 (Extended Data Fig. 6b–d and Supplementary Table 8), across cell types. Microglia, leukocytes, fibroblasts and endothelial cells showed the highest scores, elevated with both ageing (control) and AD (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d), whereas neuronal NFT was most pronounced in the patient with APOE4/4 familial AD (AD_44) (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). These findings suggest a dichotomy: senescence in non-neuronal cells may contribute to microenvironmental dysfunction in AD, whereas neuronal NFTs reflect a distinct, tau-driven pathology that escalates with disease progression or genetic susceptibility. This highlights the potential for different, cell-type-specific therapeutic targets. To ask whether these transcriptomic changes could relate to the subregion volume changes seen by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), we examined pathways regulating cell size and tissue architecture. A curated mTOR signalling gene set (core regulators MTOR, RPTOR, RHEB, TSC1/2 and DEPTOR; effectors RPS6KB1, EIF4EBP1 and SREBF1/2) showed an increased module score in AD, most prominently in non-neuronal cells (Extended Data Fig. 6e and Supplementary Table 9). Because mTORC1 regulates cell growth and size40, this raises cellular hypertrophy as one speculative contributor to the volume increases observed at the macrostructural level. Conversely, an extracellular matrix (ECM) gene set (collagens COL1A1 and COL4A1; proteoglycans ACAN, BCAN and VCAN; glycoproteins SPARC,and TNC) showed a decreased module score in AD (Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 9). These shifts suggest cell-size regulation and extracellular remodelling as candidate molecular processes potentially relevant to the subregion volume changes.

Sources indicate that microglia are central to brain ageing and neurodegeneration11,41,42. We applied trajectory inference43,44 to microglia from all conditions (young, older control participants and AD), inferring a continuous ageing-to-AD trajectory (Fig. 4d, Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 10). The pseudotime continuum was categorized into four stages: ageing phases of microglia from young participants (stage 1) and older control participants (stage 2), a late ageing phase enriched for older control participants (stage 3, representing a later state for these cells along the trajectory) and AD (stage 4) microglia (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 7a–e). A subset of microglia from older control individuals appeared at earlier trajectory points, whereas some microglia from young individuals persisted into later stages, suggesting that certain microglia may retain youthful properties whereas others show heightened susceptibility to early pathological changes.

It has been revealed that we scored three microglial signatures with UCell45 across pseudotime: (1) homeostatic (CSF1R and CX3CR1); (2) stage 1 disease-associated microglia (DAM1) (APOE and B2M), which are typically activated by ageing and amyloid plaques and (3) stage 2 DAM (DAM2) (AXL and CLEC7A), which are dependent on TREM2 signalling46,47. The scores showed a transition from homeostatic towards DAM1 with a modest DAM2 rise (Fig. 4e,f), some of which were validated in the CSF proteomics data (Extended Data Fig. 7f). This observed shift from homeostatic-to-DAM states underscores the critical role of microglial functional changes in AD progression and highlights the potential for therapeutic interventions aimed at preserving homeostatic functions or preventing the full transition to detrimental DAM states.

Sources indicate that moran’s I test identified 13,104 trajectory-associated DEGs (t-DEGs) (Supplementary Table 11 and Extended Data Fig. 7g), smoothed with RVAgene48 and clustered (Fig. 4g). Gene Ontology biological process analysis of these t-DEGs revealed that the ageing phase shifts from cilium assembly and mitochondrial morphogenesis towards stress responses, including amyloid precursor protein catabolic processes, and the disease phase shifts from cell morphogenesis and synaptic modulation to viral response pathways and protein targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum (Fig. 4h).

To test generalization beyond our cohort and the hypothalamus, we compared against the PsychAD single-nucleus atlas of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex49,50. AD-associated expression was directionally concordant across non-neuronal cell types and strongest in glia, whereas endothelial cells showed more region-specific changes consistent with the distinct vascular microenvironment of the hypothalamus (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 12). In two independent PsychAD cohorts (ageing, 208 donors49; AD, 585 donors)50, DAM signatures rose with age and AD status, recapitulating our homeostatic-to-DAM progression (Extended Data Fig. 8b–g and Supplementary Table 13). Together, these cross-cohort, cross-region comparisons indicate that the main transcriptomic signatures identified in the HypoAD hypothalamus are reproducible in independently generated datasets.

Neurons in the human hypothalamus show extensive cell-type diversity13,21,22. We analysed 213,469 neuronal nuclei, classifying them into three neurotransmitter-defined categories: inhibitory and/or γ-aminobutyric acid-ergic (GABAergic) (GAD2), excitatory and/or glutamatergic (SLC17A6) and histaminergic neurons (HDC) (Fig. 5a–c). Hierarchical Leiden clustering yielded five levels of clustering (5 to 254 subclusters). Anatomical origin was inferred from curated subregional markers21 (Extended Data Fig. 9a), with the dominant subregion listed first for subclusters expressing several markers (Extended Data Fig. 9a). A dendrogram related subtypes across resolutions, with nodes and leaves labelled by distinguishing markers. The 254 leaf subclusters were annotated by relative abundance within the total neuronal population, their distribution across young participants, older control participants and patients with AD, and inferred subregion (Fig. 5d).

For each subtype, the dendrogram is annotated with its inferred subregional identity (on the basis of marker genes) and its relative contribution from young participants, older control participants and patients with AD. e, Significant DEGs identified within the top 30 transcriptionally altered neuronal subtypes. DEGs are grouped by whether the subtype belongs to the GABAergic, glutamatergic or histaminergic category. f, Heatmap showing significantly enriched Reactome pathways within AD-altered GABAergic neurons. g, UMAP showing the 30 neuronal subtypes with the most significant transcriptional changes in early AD. Subtypes are coloured by their inferred hypothalamic subregional origin. h, Heatmap showing significantly enriched Reactome pathways within AD-altered neuronal subtypes.
