Industry observers note that the hypothalamus comprises distinct neuronal populations with specialized homeostatic roles, yet their subtype-specific contributions to AD remain poorly characterized. To address this, we performed pseudobulk differential gene expression (edgeR LRT) across the 254 neuronal subtypes, prioritizing the top 30 by DEG count, grouped by neurotransmitter category (Fig. 5e). Notably, GABAergic and/or inhibitory neurons highlighted the most pronounced changes, with enriched Reactome pathways for peptide ligand-binding receptors and G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) signalling (Fig. 5f), suggesting a potential dysregulation of neuropeptide signalling and synaptic function in the early-AD hypothalamus that may contribute to metabolic disturbances characteristic of AD pathogenesis.

Industry observers note that the top 30 subtypes were mapped by inferred subregional identity in uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) and spatial locations (Fig. 5g,h, Extended Data Fig. 9b–d and Supplementary Table 14), with other identities validated against the Visium spatial transcriptomics from nine human donors13,51 (Extended Data Fig. 10). This analysis highlighted neurons within the SCN as particularly vulnerable: a prominent SCN cluster (C254-58) revealed altered GPCR and vasopressin-related receptor pathways. Vasopressin, encoded by AVP (Extended Data Fig. 11a), is a key neuropeptide mainly synthesized and secreted by SCN neurons in a circadian manner52 and is crucial for maintaining circadian homeostasis. These findings indicate that early AD disrupts SCN neuronal function, potentially contributing to the circadian dysregulation often observed in patients.

According to recent reports, we validated our findings in the PsychAD cohort at the neuronal level, comparing cortical and hypothalamic glutamatergic and GABAergic lineages. AD-associated changes in glutamatergic neurons were more concordant across regions than in GABAergic neurons (Extended Data Fig. 11b and Supplementary Table 15), with cross-region concordance weaker for neurons than for glia, consistent with greater regional specialization of neuronal identity.

Sources indicate that we next asked how the molecular signal relates to MRI volume within matched subregions, computing per-modality area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for AD status (amyloid-positive and cognitively impaired versus all others; subregion volume for MRI; pseudobulk PC1 for snRNA-seq; Extended Data Fig. 12a–c). The modalities were concordant for some subregions and divergent for others, with no single modality uniformly superior. The SCN was more discriminative transcriptomically than by volume, consistent with its neuronal signatures described above. Imaging and transcriptomics thus provide non-redundant, regionally specific windows into hypothalamic AD pathology and combining them offers a more complete picture than either alone.

For a controlled cross-species comparison, we profiled the hypothalamus in the 5xFAD mouse model. We performed snRNA-seq on hypothalamic tissue from 8-month-old female 5xFAD mice and age-matched wild-type controls (Extended Data Fig. 13), a relatively early stage in the disease progression. The 5xFAD hypothalamus recapitulated the main DAM marker changes and immune response enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 13 and Supplementary Table 16). Neuronal subtypes and subregions were annotated with HypoMap53 (Extended Data Fig. 14). Differential expression analysis (5xFAD versus wild-type) across subregions highlighted alterations in GPCR signalling and ligand–receptor interactions within the SCN, alongside transcriptional changes in the DMH, lateral hypothalamus, ARC and paraventricular nucleus subregions (Extended Data Fig. 14 and Supplementary Table 16).

Together, these analyses reveal selective transcriptional dysregulation in specific hypothalamic neuronal subtypes and subregions in AD, with a particular impact on GABAergic and/or inhibitory neurons and the SCN. The pronounced alterations in neuropeptide signalling (for example, vasopressin) and GPCR pathways within the SCN suggest a mechanistic link to circadian rhythm disruption, a hallmark of AD that can precede cognitive decline. These findings position the hypothalamus as a critical, vulnerable hub in AD pathogenesis, advocating for therapeutic strategies that target neuropeptide-GPCR signalling, circadian entrainment or subregion-specific resilience mechanisms to potentially mitigate preclinical AD symptoms.

Sources indicate that our findings provide a multimodal view of how the hypothalamus is altered in ageing and early AD, illustrating region-specific and cell-type-specific changes that have not been observed previously. Neuroimaging studies have suggested that hypothalamic volume correlates with both ageing and cognitive decline, albeit with a relatively small effect size compared with other well-studied vulnerable brain regions54. This relative volumetric stability may reflect the region’s evolutionarily conserved nature and its critical role in survival. Here, by using a recently developed, high-resolution atlas of the human hypothalamus15, we detected specific volumetric changes in 13 distinct hypothalamic subregions that would be masked by more coarse-grained analyses with low-resolution imaging data.

It has been revealed that specifically, we found that although certain nuclei (for example, the lateral hypothalamus) diminish in size with age, others (for example, the SCN and ARC) can show an increase in volume among older adults, even when controlling for amyloid-β pathology and cognitive impairment. Together, these findings suggest that hypothalamic nuclei undergo differential volumetric changes with ageing, even in the absence of AD. However, in comparison to ageing and sex, differences in the volumes of hypothalamic nuclei in the context of amyloid-β deposition and cognitive impairment were more modest or absent. This could be related to lower early AD-related neurodegeneration in the hypothalamus compared with other brain regions or, instead, a poor sensitivity of volumetric analysis in detecting AD-related effects on the hypothalamus with limited sample size. In addition, compared with more vulnerable brain regions such as the hippocampus, the whole hypothalamus and other autonomic regions seem to remain stable with ageing, suggesting potential compensatory mechanisms conferring its resilience as it is evolutionarily conserved and vital for survival55.

In a recent development, to investigate the cellular and molecular effects of AD in individual hypothalamic nuclei, we performed snRNA-seq on post-mortem hypothalamic tissue from control donors and donors with early-stage AD, revealing key molecular features related to the inflammatory response and circadian rhythms that distinguish cells from control donors versus those from donors with AD by machine learning. Further analysis with trajectory inference and differential expression identified striking vulnerabilities in microglia, GABAergic and/or inhibitory neurons and specifically circadian rhythm and sleep-regulating neurons predicted to be from SCN and DMH. Consistent with other brain regions, microglia, which are widely recognized mediators of brain ageing and neurodegeneration2,41,42, emerged as particularly prone to transcriptional reprogramming in the hypothalamus in early AD, although our unpaired, cross-sectional data cannot establish a causal or directional relationship.

Recent findings suggest that the observed alignment of volumetric and molecular vulnerability in the SCN points to the circadian circuitry of the hypothalamus as a potentially vulnerable node in ageing and AD, placing our findings within a broader literature on circadian dysfunction in AD. Circadian disruption, including fragmented sleep–wake cycles, sundowning and altered melatonin secretion, is a well-recognized clinical feature of AD that often precedes cognitive symptoms and may accelerate disease progression8, and the SCN is the central regulator that governs these rhythms. However, because the SCN is among the subregions with lower volumetric reliability (together with mammillary body, dorsal periventricular nucleus and tuberomammillary nucleus), we interpret its volumetric association with particular caution; its involvement in our conclusions rests mainly on the orthogonal molecular evidence. We further note that resolving volume changes in these small nuclei approaches the limits of the 3T MRI-based methods used here; emerging techniques such as ultra-high-field MRI may substantially improve the reliability of subregion volumetry in vivo56. Nevertheless, our study adds converging volumetric and transcriptomic evidence that the SCN and DMH are particularly affected in ageing and AD, through dysregulated vasopressin signalling in SCN neurons, microglial inflammatory remodelling and pronounced vulnerability of GABAergic neurons implicated in circadian regulation.

Returning to the volumetric findings, our molecular data may offer candidate, although speculative, explanations for the subregion volume increases we observed with age and AD. Although these changes are small, the single-cell analyses point to several cellular mechanisms that may underlie them. Main cell-type composition in the 5xFAD whole-hypothalamus mouse data was comparable between early-AD and control animals, consistent with earlier studies with limited sample sizes in humans57,58, suggesting that the observed volumetric effects are unlikely to reflect frank gain or loss of cells, at least at this disease stage. Instead, our data implicate changes in cell size and state: we observed enrichment for ECM remodelling and mTOR signalling, which regulates cell growth, alongside inflammation signatures in non-neuronal cells. A likely contributor is reactive gliosis, which develops in the ageing hypothalamus and can manifest as apparent volume increases on structural MRI even without neuronal loss, as also reported for the hypothalamus in obesity59. Together with previous reports of neuronal hypertrophy in the human hypothalamus with age60, these changes suggest a possible link between cellular remodelling and macrostructural volume. We emphasize, however, that this link is a hypothesis rather than an established mechanism: given the large spatial-scale gap between single-nucleus transcriptomic signatures and macroscopic MRI volume, and the transcriptional noise inherent to snRNA-seq, it cannot be inferred from the transcriptomic data alone and would require spatially resolved protein or histological validation. More fundamentally, fully unifying the two modalities remains challenging. Because the volumetric and molecular data derive from separate cohorts without paired, coregistered measurements in the same individuals, we did not attempt coupled statistical integration, such as multimodal embedding or the prediction of molecular state from imaging features. Instead, we compared the AD-predictive signal of each modality at matched anatomical subregions, revealing that imaging and transcriptomics provide non-redundant and regionally specific windows into hypothalamic pathology (Extended Data Fig. 12a–c). True integration, in which volumetric and molecular features are jointly modelled in a shared statistical framework, will require future studies that acquire both modalities from the same individuals, ideally with spatially coregistered sampling.

In a recent development, in summary, our combined volumetric and single-cell atlas of the human hypothalamus provides a high-resolution framework for elucidating how ageing and AD pathology differentially affect specific hypothalamic subregions and cell types. We highlight notable vulnerabilities in GABAergic and/or inhibitory neurons, SCN and DMH circadian regulators, and inflammatory microglial cascades, underscoring their potential roles in instigating early hypothalamic dysfunction.

The brain MRI scans used in this study were obtained from two separate datasets. The first was from the AMBR study16. A second dataset from the CBA study17 was added to improve rigour and reproducibility. Both studies obtained 0.8-mm isotropic T1 magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo and T2 sampling perfection with application-optimized contrasts using different flip-angle evolution sequences for segmentation and volumetric analysis of specific hypothalamic nuclei as described in ref. 15. Although several other high-resolution brain MRI datasets exist, the AMBR and CBA studies also obtained assessments of brain amyloid-β deposition and cognitive impairment. Differences in other aspects of the AMBR and CBA studies, such as cohort characteristics, were seen as valuable to improve the robustness and generalizability of this study. Test–retest reliability of the segmentation pipeline was assessed using the ICC ((2,1); two-way random effects, absolute agreement, single measurement) in eight participants with repeat scans in the CBA study. Following ref. 61, we classified ICC < 0.40 as poor and 0.40–0.59 as fair; we note that other schemes, such as ref. 62, place the poor–moderate boundary at 0.50. For structures with poor ICC, we later corroborate the volumetric findings with a complementary molecular modality. All associations reported here are based on bilateral (combined left and right) volumes; hemisphere-specific measures, which are inherently noisier, were examined only descriptively and did not form the basis of our conclusions.

To specifically assess the effect of AD on subregion volumes, participants were categorized on the basis of their amyloid-β and cognitive status. Amyloid status was determined from amyloid positron emission tomography imaging or CSF biomarker assessments when available using study-specific criteria: in AMBR, labelling was based on Knight Alzheimer Disease Research Center (ADRC) cut-offs for [carbon-11]-Pittsburgh compound B (C-11 PiB) standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR), [fluorine-18]-florbetapir (F-18 AV-45) SUVR, by visual read when SUVR data were not available, or by CSF test results. In the CBA study, labelling was based on provided centiloid values thresholded at 16.4, corresponding to the Knight ADRC C-11 PiB mean cortical SUVR cut-off of 1.42 (ref. 63). If amyloid-β status was positive any time before or up to 1 year after the MRI, it was labelled as positive. Conversely if amyloid-β status was negative any time after or up to 1  year before the MRI, it was labelled as negative. Otherwise amyloid-β status was considered not available (NA).

Cognitive status was labelled as ‘impaired’ or ‘unimpaired’ using study-specific criteria. In the AMBR study, labelling was based on the Clinical Dementia Rating scale (CDR), with CDR = 0 indicating cognitively unimpaired and CDR > 0 indicating cognitive impairment. A subject was labelled as impaired only if assessed as impaired within ±1 year of the MRI, and as unimpaired only if assessed as unimpaired at any time after the MRI or within 1 year before (otherwise coded as NA). In the CBA study, labelling was based on the timepoint-specific diagnosis code, with code 1 indicating cognitively unimpaired; codes 2, 4, 5 and 6 indicating evidence of cognitive impairment and code 3 (subjective impairment) coded as NA.

In both studies, individuals meeting criteria for both cognitive impairment and positive amyloid-β status were designated as the AD group. Conversely, participants without cognitive deficits and with negative amyloid-β status were classified as the non-AD (control) group. To minimize potential confounding from intermediate pathology profiles, only individuals clearly falling into these AD or non-AD categories were included in these specific comparative analyses. The cohort had a mean age of 63.4 ± 11.6 years (mean ± standard deviation) and included 60.5% women. Moreover, our dataset includes information directly relevant to AD, including 30.6% with abnormal cognitive status and 13.8% who were amyloid-β positive (Extended Data Fig. 1a). The mean total hypothalamic volume for this cohort was 736.2 ± 88.2 mm3.

Given that the dataset did not have predefined group structures for all desired comparisons, we used a GLM to assess the associations between hypothalamic subregion volumes (summed across left and right hemispheres) and various demographic and clinical variables.

Specifically, in the AMBR study (n = 202), we modelled (denoted as ‘~’) the natural logarithm of each subregion’s volume (log[subregion volume]) as a function of scaled age at MRI, sex, cognitive (cogn.) status, amyloid-β deposition status and other relevant covariates, where ‘+’ denotes additive main effects, ‘:’ denotes an interaction, ‘×’ denotes crossed terms (main effects plus their interaction), and ‘scale()’ denotes z-score standardization of a covariate:.

P values for individual variables from the GLM analyses were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR).

In the CBA study (n = 256), the metabolic and sleep covariates (body mass index (BMI)), HgbA1c and Epworth Sleepiness Score) were not available; we therefore modelled the natural logarithm of each subregion’s volume (log[subregion volume]) as a function of scaled age at MRI, sex, cognitive status, amyloid-β deposition status, their interaction and ICV:.

In the harmonized two-study pooled cohort (AMBR + CBA, n = 458), we modelled the natural logarithm of each subregion’s volume as a function of scaled age at MRI, sex, cognitive status, amyloid-β deposition status, their interaction, ICV and study of origin. The metabolic and sleep covariates above were not included here as they were not available across both studies:.

To test whether the association between age and subregion volume differed by disease status, we fitted a separate GLM that included an age × group interaction term, where group distinguished cognitively normal, amyloid-negative individuals from all others:.

According to recent reports, to compare subregion volumes between patients with AD and non-AD individuals while balancing demographic differences, we constructed a logistic regression model to estimate each participant’s propensity score for AD-group membership, using sex and age at MRI as covariates. Propensity-score matching was then performed using a nearest-neighbour algorithm, generating matched pairs of patients with AD and non-AD individuals with similar distributions of sex and age. This balanced these key covariates between groups for the subsequent volumetric comparisons.

To evaluate the predictive power of hypothalamic volumes in identifying AD and cognitive status, we conducted a series of binary classification tasks using receiver-operating-characteristic analysis. Three primary target conditions were defined: (1) cognitive status (impaired ‘A’ versus normal ‘N’), (2) amyloid status (positive ‘P’ versus negative ‘N’) and (3) a composite AD group (A+P+ versus all others). For each condition, we compared the diagnostic performance of two distinct feature sets: a multivariate model comprising 13 individual hypothalamic subregions (ARC, anterior hypothalamic area, dorsal periventricular nucleus, DMH, lateral hypothalamus, medial preoptic nucleusMPO, paraventricular nucleus, posterior hypothalamus, periventricular nucleus, SCN, supraoptic nucleus, tuberomammillary nucleus, ventromedial nucleus) and a univariate model using only the total hypothalamic volume. Classification was performed using logistic regression with balanced class weights to account for potential group size discrepancies. Model performance was validated using a fivefold stratified cross-validation approach. Features were standardized (z-score normalized) within each training fold before model fitting. The resulting area under the curve was calculated as the mean across cross-validation folds, with the standard deviation reported as a measure of model stability.

Given the central role of the hypothalamus in energy homeostasis and metabolic regulation, we examined whether BMI was associated with hypothalamic volume at the total and subregion level. BMI was not significantly associated with total hypothalamic volume (estimate ± s.e. = −0.005 ± 0.007, adjusted P = 0.505, Extended Data Fig. 2e and Supplementary Table 4) or with any bilateral subregion volume after FDR correction (all adjusted P > 0.086). In lateralized analyses, the left DMH demonstrated a significant negative association with BMI (left DMH −0.042 ± 0.014, adjusted P = 0.014), although this was not observed on the right side (right DMH −0.010 ± 0.018, adjusted P = 0.664, Extended Data Fig. 2e and Supplementary Table 4).

Unfixed, flash-frozen half-hypothalamus tissues were obtained from the Netherlands Brain Bank (NBB), Netherlands Institute for Neuroscience, Amsterdam (open access at www.brainbank.nl). All material has been collected from donors for or from whom a written informed consent for a brain autopsy and the use of the material and clinical information for research purposes had been obtained by the NBB.

This consent procedure was approved by the Ethical Committee of the VU University Medical Center (Vrije Universiteit, Amsterdam, the Netherlands), independently and before this study. Tissue blocks were stored at −80 °C.

The cohort comprised 14 donors: 7 control participants without dementia and 7 patients with AD (6 sporadic and 1 familial). Comorbidities were common in both groups and predominantly cardiovascular; control participants also included donors with malignancy (colorectal carcinoma, multiple myeloma, melanoma), whereas the AD group included one donor each with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and bladder carcinoma. Causes of death included acute cardiac events and pulmonary embolism (control participants), euthanasia (2 control participants), end-stage malignancy (control participants) and respiratory insufficiency, aspiration pneumonia, cachexia, ileus and dehydration due to swallowing problems (AD patients). No donor had a documented intensive care unit admission; all deaths occurred in community, nursing home or palliative care settings. All key determinants of post-mortem gene expression quality (age, post-mortem interval, brain pH, RNA integrity number and agonal state estimated from clinical records) were comparable between groups (all P > 0.1 with Mann–Whitney U test). All samples indicated high quality, with short post-mortem intervals of less than 9 h and RNA integrity number scores above 6.5. Full donor-level clinical and neuropathological details can be requested from the NBB using the NBB ID, which is available on request.

According to recent reports, to overcome the input cell number limits of droplet-based single-cell sequencing (which typically captures tens of thousands of cells per sample) relative to the vast cellularity of the entire hypothalamus, we performed targeted macrodissection. In this initial study, we prioritized in-depth profiling of three subregions already implicated in ageing and AD over a shallower survey of the whole hypothalamus: the ARC, a hub for energy homeostasis housing pro-opiomelanocortin and agouti-related peptide neurons that integrate leptin and insulin signals64,65; the SCN, the master circadian pacemaker whose disruption underlies sleep–wake disturbances among the earliest non-cognitive symptoms of AD66,67; and the mammillary nucleus, a component of the Papez memory circuit disproportionately vulnerable to neurodegeneration in AD models10. Together, these subregions span the anterior–posterior extent of the hypothalamus and represent three of its main functional domains: metabolic control, circadian regulation, and memory circuitry. Focusing on three primary regions of interest, the ARC, SCN and mammillary nucleus, prevented the severe dilution of rare neuronal populations, ensuring sufficient sampling depth for downstream differential expression analysis. Macrodissection was performed on hemisected hypothalami within a Leica cryostat at the lowest temperature setting, with the tissue surrounded by dry ice. To maintain RNA integrity and prevent cross-contamination, the blade and all dissection tools were sanitized and treated with RNaseZap RNase Decontamination Solution between each sample.

Wild-type and heterozygous (8-month-old) 5xFAD-C57BL/6 female mice were obtained from The Jackson Laboratory. Mice were housed and used according to protocols approved by Brown University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and in accordance with institutional and national guidelines. Animals were housed at 21 ± 1 °C (70 ± 2 °F) with humidity from 50% to 70%. Animals were fed ad libitum Lab Diet 5010 chow and water. The light cycle was 12 h on 12 h off and lights were on between 7:00 and 19:00. Animals were exposed to male bedding 3 d before being euthanized to synchronize the oestrous cycle. Animals were euthanized at Zeitgeber time ZT2–ZT3. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size. Animals were not randomly allocated to experimental groups. Investigators were not blinded to group allocation during the experiments or outcome assessment.

No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes, but our donor numbers are comparable to those of established snRNA-seq studies of the human brain in AD, which typically profiled 3–10 donors per group68,69,70. Individual nuclei were excluded from analysis on the basis of quality control metrics (feature count and mitochondrial read count). Data collection and analysis were not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

Nuclei extraction was performed using the Nuclei PURE Prep kit (Millipore Sigma) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. All procedures were performed in the cold room before the 45-min spin down. Tissue was transferred using a transfer pipette into a refrigerated Dounce homogenizer with 5 ml of lysis solution following kit instructions. Tissue was homogenized with the Dounce B and the lysate was transferred into a 15-ml Falcon tube through a 40-μm filter. The sucrose purification step was performed with the modifications that half the volume of all reagents was used to account for the small tissue sample sizes, an SW34 rotor was used and samples were spun for 45 min at 30,000g (13,000 r.p.m.) at 4 °C.

Nuclei were counted using a hemocytometer and 10,000 nuclei per sample were loaded onto the Chromium Single Cell 3′ Chip (10x Genomics) and processed with the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics). Samples were sequenced at GENEWIZ on an Illumina NovaSeq, with a target of 50,000 reads per sample.

Sequence alignment for human snRNA-seq data (including the dataset from ref. 22) was performed against the GRCh38 (2020) reference genome. These alignments were executed using Cell Ranger (10x Genomics; v.7.1.0 for human) with the --include-introns flag, essential for capturing nuclear RNA.

In a recent development, following alignment, systematic background noise, such as ambient RNA, was removed from the count matrices using CellBender (v.0.3.0)71. For quality control, outlier cells were identified on the basis of established criteria. Specifically, cells were flagged as outliers if they exceeded 5 median absolute deviations for any of the following quality control metrics: log1p_total_counts, log1p_n_genes_by_counts or pct_counts_in_top_20_genes. In addition, cells with a mitochondrial transcript percentage of 10% or more were excluded.

According to recent reports, potential doublets (two or more cells captured as a single droplet) were then identified and filtered out using scDblFinder72. After these quality control steps, data from different individuals were integrated using single-cell variational inference23 to correct for batch effects. Subsequent data visualization and downstream analyses were performed using tools from the Seurat73 and Scanpy74 ecosystems.

Subregional samples were never pooled. Each donor contributed three tissue samples obtained by macrodissection enriching for distinct hypothalamic subregions (ARC, SCN, MN), yielding 42 samples across the 14 older donors. Each sample was collected into a separate tube and processed through an independent 10x Chromium channel, producing independent library preparations and therefore constituting a biologically and technically independent observation capturing distinct cellular compositions and independent sources of technical variation.

Differential expression analysis was performed using a pseudobulk approach with the LRT in edgeR75. Genes were significant if the Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P value was below 0.05. The three young reference donors22 were included only to anchor cell-type annotation and the microglial ageing trajectory; all AD-versus-control differentially expression analysis was restricted to the HypoAD cohort, excluding the familial AD (AD_44) donor.

GSEA was performed using the fgsea package76 with the hallmark gene-set lists and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) and Reactome gene-set list from Molecular Signatures Database76,77. For GSEA input, genes within each cluster were ranked by their log2 fold change (log2[FC]) values, determined from edgeR LRT differentially expressed analysis. The GSEA was then performed using the fgseaMultilevel() command with default settings. Gene sets were considered significantly enriched if the adjusted P < 0.1.

To contextualize our data within a broader reference, we used a universal cell embedding (UCE) foundation model. UCE projects single-cell gene expression profiles into a universal embedding space that is agnostic to technical covariates such as batch effects or protocol differences78. We implemented the 33-layer version of UCE as specified in its official repository (https://github.com/snap-stanford/UCE), using Python (v.3.9.0) and PyTorch (v.2.1.1), with the publicly available pretrained model weights.

Sources indicate that we then used UCE to project our control and AD snRNA-seq datasets into a shared embedding space alongside a publicly available, community-curated human brain atlas containing more than 25 million cells78. The resulting embeddings were visualized in a two-dimensional UMAP space to benchmark our newly generated data against this large-scale public reference.

To identify predictive features for the classification task distinguishing cells from AD versus control individuals, we developed and applied a machine learning pipeline using Python (v.3.10.9) and the scikit-learn library (v.1.6.1). The full pipeline is available through GitHub (https://github.com/Webb-Laboratory/HypoAD).

For cell-type-specific models, the full dataset was filtered to include only cells corresponding to a single target cell type (for example, Neuron, Astrocyte), on the basis of predefined annotations.

According to recent reports, we used a leave-one-batch-out nested cross-validation strategy to ensure robust hyperparameter tuning, prevent data leakage and give an unbiased performance evaluation. For each of the seven outer folds, an inner sixfold cross-validation was used to tune the model’s hyperparameters. This approach generated seven distinct models, from which we ranked gene-associated weights to identify the most predictive features (Fig. 3a). Specifically, the data for all cells, as well as for each of the top five most abundant cell types, were split into seven outer folds on the basis of the sample batch of origin (leave-one-batch-out). Each batch comprised two donors (one control and one AD), and no donor appeared in more than one batch. For each outer fold, the test set consisted of nuclei from a single held-out batch, such that both donors in that batch were entirely unseen during training. The remaining six batches were used for an inner leave-one-batch-out cross-validation to select the optimal hyperparameters for an Elastic Net logistic regression model. The 5 × 5 hyperparameter grid included a logarithmic search for the regularization parameter C (from 10−2 to 102) and a linear search for the L1 ratio (from 0 to 1). The model with the best average inner-fold AUROC was then retrained on all six training batches and evaluated on the held-out test batch. We first trained a model on all cells, which achieved predictive performance (average AUROC = 0.75). We then trained models specific to the five most abundant cell types. All cell-type-specific models also performed well, with the microglia model showing the highest accuracy (average AUROC = 0.91). The comparatively lower performance for neuronal models may be attributable to the complexity and heterogeneity of neurons in the hypothalamus (Fig. 3b).

After completing the outer cross-validation, we extracted the feature weights (coefficients) from the seven models, each trained on one outer fold. Two feature ranking lists were generated for each cell type. The ‘raw-weight’ rank was created by ranking all features on the basis of their mean weight across the seven folds, preserving the sign to indicate positive or negative prediction association. The ‘absolute-weight’ rank was created by ranking features on the basis of the mean of their absolute weights to measure overall predictive importance regardless of direction.

According to recent reports, to identify features consistently important across all cell types, we defined a ‘shared score’ for each gene as the mean of its absolute-weight rank across the five cell types analysed, and coloured by its direction (that is, whether the feature is on the top or bottom of the raw-weight rank list). Cell-type-specific ranks for features were defined by inquiry_rank/mean_rank_others.

In a recent development, to identify biological pathways associated with our model’s predictions, we performed preranked GSEA using the gseapy (v.1.1.9) Python package. For each cell type, the full list of features was ranked using the mean raw weight. This ranked list was tested for enrichment against the KEGG pathway database (v.2021), Hallmark (v.2020) and Gene Ontology Biological Process (2021) from the Molecular Signatures Database. Significance was determined using a permutation-based test (1,000 permutations), and pathways with FDR q < 0.05 were considered significantly enriched.

To infer the ageing process for the microglia cluster (n = 51,420 nuclei) generated in Seurat, we applied Monocle3 (refs. 43,44). Monocle3 typically uses dimensionality reduction to position cells in a lower-dimensional space, can correct for batch effects using mutual nearest-neighbour alignment and subsequently connects cells to construct trajectories in a semi-supervised manner.

Recent findings suggest that for our analysis of the microglia–macrophage cluster, we directly used the integrated Seurat object, bypassing any further batch correction or dimensionality reduction steps within Monocle3 itself, as these had been addressed in the previous Seurat processing. After subsetting the microglia cluster, the root of the trajectory was programmatically defined by selecting the principal graph node most enriched for cells originating from young individuals. The horizontal axis in Fig. 4e represents a data-driven transcriptomic pseudotime learned from the single-cell data, not a chronological timeline, and individual donors do not necessarily follow this ordering. Trajectory-based expression analysis along this inferred trajectory was then performed using Moran’s I test, as implemented in Monocle3. Genes with a q value (FDR-adjusted P value) of less than 0.01 were considered significantly trajectory dependent, resulting in the identification of 13,104 such genes.

It has been revealed that functional enrichment analysis of the 13,104 t-DEGs, grouped into individual expression groups identified through co-expression analysis, was performed using Enrichr (v.3.0)79. This analysis used the GO_Biological_Process_2018 gene-set database. Statistically significantly enriched Gene Ontology terms were identified on the basis of a Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted P value (Padj) < 0.01. For visualization purposes, the top ten significantly enriched terms per group were shown in a dot plot.

Sources indicate that to decode and visualize the dynamic expression patterns of the t-DEGs (n = 13,104) along the inferred pseudotime trajectory, we used the RVAgene package (v.1.0)48 in Python (v.3.9.6) with PyTorch (v.1.9.0). Before input into RVAgene, expression values for each gene were averaged within discrete pseudotime bins and subsequently rescaled to a range of [−1, 1]. The RVAgene neural network was configured with a symmetrical architecture comprising two hidden layers (48 nodes per layer) and two latent variable dimensions. The smoothed, reconstructed expression trajectories of the t-DEGs generated by RVAgene were then used to create the summary heatmap.

Two gene sets were assembled to score mTOR(PI3K-AKT-mTOR) signalling and ECM (matrisome) activity. Each set began from a curated list of canonical genes: for mTOR, core pathway components and downstream lipid–sterol effectors; for ECM, matrisome constituents, including collagens, laminins, proteoglycans, matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors (MMPs or TIMPs) and ADAMTS proteases. Each seed list was expanded by gene-symbol pattern matching (for example, COL[0–9] + A[0–9], MMP[0–9], LAM[ABC][0–9]) and filtered to remove unrelated ‘look-alike’ families (for example, mitochondrial import genes TIMM/TOMM, TIMELESS), then restricted to genes detected in the dataset, yielding 70 mTOR and 157 ECM genes (Supplementary Table 9, tabs mTOR_set and ECM_set).

In a recent development, counts were normalized with Seurat’s NormalizeData (log-normalization, scale factor 10,000). Per-cell module scores were computed with Seurat’s AddModuleScore (default parameters: 24 expression bins, control pools of 100 randomly sampled genes per set gene), which subtracts the mean expression of a randomly selected control gene set from the mean expression of the target set. mTOR and ECM scores were calculated jointly (Score1 = mTOR, Score2 = ECM). For statistical testing, donors were grouped as young, control or AD. To avoid pseudoreplication, per-cell scores were aggregated to the sample level by taking the mean score across all cells of a given cell type within each sample, retaining only sample × cell-type combinations with ten or more cells. For each cell type and gene set, module scores were compared between control and AD samples using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons across all cell type × gene-set tests using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Analyses were performed in R with Seurat and rstatix.

Recent findings suggest that cell2location is a Bayesian model that uses snRNA-seq cell-type signatures to infer cell types in Visium spatial transcriptomics by decomposing messenger RNA counts in each Visium voxel into cell types. We performed the three main steps in the cell2location workflow: estimating reference expression signatures of cell types using our dataset, mapping the learned cell-type signatures onto the slides, and performing downstream analysis. The code, model parameters and training evaluations can be found in the Jupyter notebooks in our GitHub repository. In brief, we used the default parameters to train the cell2location model.

Sources indicate that lumbar CSF samples from a cohort of 280 participants (including healthy control, AD and other conditions) were analysed by means of liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Samples were processed on a Thermo EASY-nLC 1200 system coupled to a Thermo Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid mass spectrometer. Detailed chromatography and data acquisition parameters follow the methods described in ref. 80. Quality control was maintained using inter-batch and inter-experiment samples across 96-well plates to evaluate and correct for technical effects. Protein quantification was performed by mapping raw spectra to an empirically corrected Prosit81 library (generated by means of gas-phase fractionated, narrow-window injections) using EncyclopeDIA, with peak integration and protein mapping finalized in Skyline.

Industry observers note that differential abundance analysis was performed to compare patients with AD (n = 19) against the healthy control group (n = 205) using the limma and eBayes framework82 on the preprocessed and log2 normalized protein quantification table in R. Statistical significance for differential protein abundance was defined by Padj < 0.05.

In a recent development, to validate cell-type-specific transcriptomic signatures at the protein level, significant CSF proteins were intersected with significant DEGs from single-cell pseudobulk analysis (Padj < 0.05). To address nomenclature inconsistencies between modalities, a ‘fuzzy-join’ logic was implemented. This approach matched protein symbols to RNA symbols on the basis of exact matches, prefix alignment and antisense transcript identification.

Validation of nine ageing-related and AD-related markers from the microglia pseudotime analysis (CSF1R, CX3CR1, P2RY12, APOE, B2M, CTSB, AXL, CLEC7A and TIMP2 in Fig. 4f) was performed by extracting their corresponding features from the CSF proteomics expression matrix using case-insensitive substring matching. To isolate age-related versus disease-related protein trajectories, the healthy control cohort was further stratified into ‘young’ (less than 65 years of age) and ‘aged’ (65 years or older) subgroups and visualized accordingly. Statistical analysis did not show significant differences between the groups, despite the protein trajectories’ showing trends similar to the gene expression data.

AD-associated transcriptomic signatures were validated against the PsychAD Consortium single-nucleus RNA-seq resource of the human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Mount Sinai Brain Bank cohort), obtained from CELLxGENE Discover (https://cellxgene.cziscience.com/collections/84ce6837-548d-4a1f-919f-0bc0d9a3952f). Two releases were used: an AD-enriched cohort for disease comparisons and a neurologically normal cohort spanning adulthood for the ageing analysis. For all analyses, Ensembl gene IDs were mapped to HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee symbols using the feature_name field supplied with the dataset, and raw counts were normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and log1p-transformed.

According to recent reports, for cross-cohort differential expression concordance, PsychAD cell types were mapped to their HypoAD counterparts at the main cell-type level. Non-neuronal populations (astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, OPCs and endothelial cells) were assigned direct one-to-one correspondences. Because neuronal subtypes are largely region-specific and the cortical subtypes annotated in PsychAD do not correspond one-to-one to hypothalamic populations, the finer PsychAD neuronal subtypes were aggregated into glutamatergic and GABAergic (GABA) lineages; for each gene, the subtype result with the lowest FDR was taken as the representative statistic for the lineage. Pseudobulk differential expression (AD versus control) was computed per cell type with edgeR and compared across datasets by plotting the paired log2[FC] of shared genes. Directional concordance of AD-associated changes was quantified with Spearman’s rank correlation (ρ) on the subset of genes significantly differentially expressed (FDR < 0.05) in both datasets.

Sources indicate that for microglial DAM module scoring, module scores for homeostatic microglia (HEXB, CST3, CX3CR1, CSF1R, CTSS, TMSB4X, P2RY12, C1QB), DAM1 (TYROBP, CTSB, APOE, B2M, FTH1, TREM2) and DAM2 (TREM2, AXL, CST7, CTSL, LPL, CD9, CSF1, ITGAX, CLEC7A, LILRB4, TIMP2) were computed with scanpy.tl.score_genes (analogous to Seurat’s AddModuleScore). In the ageing cohort, scores were averaged per donor and then per age bin, correlated with age by Spearman’s ρ and shown with locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (bandwidth 0.6); individual representative genes were shown as scatter plots against donor age (locally weighted scatterplot smoothing bandwidth 0.5) and as violin plots comparing donors less than 65 years of age versus those 65 years of age or older. In the AD cohort, the same gene-level visualizations were produced across the four donor groups (young, control, AD and familial AD).

AMBR-MRIs were obtained from studies involving positron emission tomography imaging that were approved by the Radioactive Drug Research Committee and the Institutional Review Board at Washington University in St. Louis. All participants provided written consent. CBA-MRI studies involving human participants were reviewed and approved by the Human Research Protection Office at the University of Pittsburgh. All participants provided written informed consent to participate17. All procedures and research protocols for post-mortem tissue were approved by the Institutional Review Board at Brown University. All research was performed in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. Informed consent for the use of post-mortem tissue was obtained from all donors or their next of kin.

In a recent development, a, Characteristics of the two studies. b, Test–retest ICC(2,1) for bilateral, left and right regional volumes (two-way random-effects, absolute agreement, single measurement). Points are ICC estimates. Bars show 95% confidence intervals computed by irr::icc. n = 8 independent participants, each scanned twice (16 scans, paired measurements). Red indicates ICC < 0.4. c, Pearson correlation heatmap of hypothalamic structure volumes and age at MRI in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants (n = 165 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across all pairwise correlations (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). d, Age–volume Pearson r in cognitively normal, amyloid-negative participants, analysed as pooled (black, n = 165), CBA (orange, n = 91) and AMBR (blue, n = 74) samples. Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across 26 age–volume correlations per analysis. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05, open circles non-significance. e, Associations of age, female sex and intracranial volume with subregion volumes in AMBR, CBA and pooled participants. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients. Bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × s.e.). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in pooled models. Two-sided t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. BH correction covered 26 regions per predictor and cohort. Exact estimates, intervals, t statistics, degrees of freedom and raw/adjusted P are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

a, Pearson correlation heatmap of extrahypothalamic volumes and age at MRI (n = 458 independent participants). Blue and red indicate positive and negative correlations, respectively. Two-sided Pearson tests used Benjamini–Hochberg (BH) correction across unique pairwise correlations within the matrix (*adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001). b, Age–volume Pearson correlations in the pooled cohort (n = 458 independent participants), CBA (n = 256) and AMBR (n = 202). Two-sided Pearson tests used BH correction across all 26 regional age–volume correlations within each cohort. Filled circles indicate adjusted P < 0.05. Open circles indicate adjusted P ≥ 0.05. c, Forest plots of Gaussian GLM coefficients for hypothalamic (top) and extrahypothalamic (bottom) volumes, ordered by coefficient estimate. Points show fitted coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 316 independent participants in every model, with covariates as in Fig. 1c. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 308 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all eight coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Point color and size indicate adjusted significance. d, Age, female sex and intracranial volume coefficients for extrahypothalamic structures. Points show Gaussian GLM coefficients and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). Every regional model used 107 AMBR, 209 CBA or 316 pooled independent participants. Models included age, sex, cognition, amyloid-β, cognition × amyloid-β and intracranial volume, plus study in the pooled analysis. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 100, 202 and 308 residual degrees of freedom, respectively. P values were BH-adjusted across 26 regions separately for each predictor and cohort. e, Body mass index (BMI) associations in AMBR-only Gaussian GLMs. Points show BMI coefficients per SD of BMI and bars show unadjusted approximate 95% confidence intervals (estimate ± 1.96 × SE). n = 174 independent participants in each regional model. Models adjusted for age, sex, cognition, amyloid status, cognition × amyloid status, HbA1c, Epworth sleepiness score and intracranial volume. Two-sided coefficient t-tests used 164 residual degrees of freedom. BH adjustment covered all ten model coefficients, including the intercept, within each regional model. Exact results for all panels are in Supplementary Tables 2–4. In the figure panels, AN denotes the arcuate nucleus (ARC in the main text) and DM denotes the dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH in the main text).

Sources indicate that a, PCA of 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structure volumes (n = 458 participants). Scatter plots are colored by eight covariates: age, sex, amyloid-β status, cognitive status, intracranial volume (ICV), total brain volume (TBV), study and amyloid days. Three variants are shown: raw volumes (top, PC1 = 44.2%, PC2 = 14.4%), fully residualized for age, sex, ICV, TBV and study (middle, PC1 = 27.6%, PC2 = 13.1%), and partially residualized for sex, ICV, TBV and study (bottom, PC1 = 27.4%, PC2 = 13.9%). b–c, PC1 and PC2 loadings from raw (b) and fully residualized (c) PCA. Bars are red for negative loadings and teal for positive loadings. d, Changes in PC1 (left) and PC2 (right) loadings from raw (orange) to fully residualized (green) PCA, shown as dumbbell plots ordered by magnitude of change. e, Associations of PC1–PC5 scores with nine covariates in raw and partially residualized PCA. Continuous covariates were tested using two-sided Pearson correlations, with r2 as effect size. Categorical covariates were tested using omnibus one-way ANOVA F-tests, with η2 as effect size and an upper-tail F reference distribution. P values were Benjamini–Hochberg (BH)-adjusted across 45 PC–covariate tests separately for each PCA variant. n = 458 participants, with data available for cognitive status in 422, amyloid-β status in 340, CogDays in 441 and AmyloidDays in 358. *Adjusted P < 0.05, **adjusted P < 0.01, ***adjusted P < 0.001. f, Regional volume versus age in n = 181 independent male participants. Each point represents one participant, colored by combined cognitive and amyloid status (black, missing status). Black LOESS curves estimate conditional mean volume. Shading highlights pointwise 95% confidence intervals for the fitted curves, rather than between-participant standard deviations. g, Regional volume distributions after nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching of AD and cognitively unimpaired, amyloid-negative participants on sex and age. The pooled comparison includes 24 AD participants (18 men, 6 women) and 24 matched controls (16 men, 8 women). Center lines show medians, box bounds the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range of the box bounds. Dots represent individual participants, including observations beyond the whiskers. Duplicate outlier symbols are suppressed. h, ROC curves from class-balanced logistic regression with five-fold stratified cross-validation, using 13 hypothalamic subregion volumes or total hypothalamic volume to predict cognitive impairment (n = 422 participants, 140 impaired, 282 unimpaired), amyloid positivity (n = 340, 63 positive, 277 negative) and AD status (n = 316, 24 AD, 292 others). AUCs are mean ± standard deviation across five folds. The subregion model had a higher mean AUC for all three outcomes. No formal comparison was performed. i, Univariate ROC curves predicting AD status from 25 hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structures and total hypothalamic volume (n = 316 participants, 24 AD, 292 others), sorted by descending AUC. The arcuate nucleus (AN; ARC in the main text), fornix (fx), paraventricular nucleus (Pa) and ventromedial nucleus (VM) were the strongest predictors. When lower volume predicted AD (indicated by “−”), scores were sign-inverted before ROC calculation.

a, Donor metadata. The table summarizes condition, age, Braak stage, APOE genotype, amyloid-β status, postmortem delay (PMD), RNA integrity number (RIN) and time of death for each donor. Accompanying heatmaps show donors clustered by pathology metrics (left) and quality metrics (right), with annotation bars indicating condition, time of death, pathology and quality. b, UMAP showing nuclei from this study embedded within a reference atlas of 25 million publicly available human brain cells, colored by major cell type and condition. c, UMAP of the integrated dataset following scVI batch correction, with nuclei colored by condition, batch, individual, and inclusion of the Siletti et al. dataset. d, Boxplots of the per-tissue-sample mean number of genes detected per nucleus, stratified by cell type and condition. Each tissue sample is one hypothalamic subregion from one donor. The center line is the median, box bounds are the 25th and 75th percentiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme observations within 1.5 × the interquartile range of the box bounds. Observations beyond the whiskers are shown as points. CTL and AD contain seven donors each (AD includes the familial case). Young reference samples derive from three donors, except young epithelial cells, which derive from one donor. In cell-type order neuron, epithelial, endothelial, ependymal, OPC, astrocyte, fibroblast, oligodendrocyte, microglia, and leukocyte, n (CTL/AD/young tissue samples) is 21/21/24, 8/4/2, 21/21/19, 19/17/19, 21/21/24, 21/21/24, 21/21/23, 21/21/24, 21/21/22 and 21/21/19. The epithelial samples come from four CTL and three AD donors. These are descriptive summaries, and no inferential test is shown. e, Boxplots of the per-tissue-sample mean UMI count per nucleus, with the same samples and group sizes as d. Boxplot elements are as in d. The y-axis is logarithmic. No inferential comparison is presented. f, Stacked bar plots showing cell-type composition for samples from each hypothalamic subregion (SCN, MN, and ARC). g, Bar plot quantifying the total number of nuclei for each cell type in the final dataset.

Industry observers note that selected significantly enriched Hallmark (top) and Gene Ontology biological process (GO:BP; bottom) pathways from GSEA. The x-axis represents the absolute NES, dot size represents the number of genes in a pathway, and color indicates significance (−log10[FDR]).

In a recent development, a, Top row: violin plots displaying significant DEGs across specific major cell types (endothelial cells, microglia, and OPCs) from snRNA-seq, comparing CTL and AD individuals. Bottom row: boxplots illustrating the normalized log2 abundance of the corresponding significant differentially abundant proteins (DAPs) in CSF, comparing healthy controls (HC) with AD patients. Statistical significance with BH correction is indicated by asterisks (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001). b, UMAP projections illustrating the expression scores for three senescence-related and three NFT-related gene signatures across all nuclei. c, Violin plots comparing the expression scores of three NFT-related signatures across major cell types. Per-sample mean UCell scores for the NFT Orr signature were higher in AD than control (Wilcoxon rank-sum test on 18 AD versus 21 control samples, BH-adjusted across cell types: microglia P = 0.037, OPC P = 0.025). d, Violin plots showing the expression of key senescence-related genes (CDKN1A, canonical; CALR, responses; SOD2, initiators) across major cell types. Pseudobulk edgeR-LRT false discovery rate (FDR) is indicated by asterisks (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001). e–f, Module scores for the mTOR signaling (e) and extracellular matrix (ECM; f) gene sets, comparing control and AD donors at the sample level, stratified by cell type. Scores were computed using Seurat’s AddModuleScore (background-corrected mean expression relative to randomly sampled control gene sets matched by expression level). Each point represents the mean per-sample score for a given cell type (minimum 10 cells per sample). Boxes show median and IQR; whiskers extend to 1.5 × IQR. Brackets indicate pairwise comparisons with BH-adjusted significance (Wilcoxon rank-sum test).

a, Split UMAP embeddings of hypothalamic microglia/macrophage nuclei by group: young, 3,213 nuclei (3 donors), CTL, 24,648 (7 donors), AD, 20,087 (6 donors), and AD_44, 3,472 (1 donor), totaling 51,420 nuclei. In each panel, the full population is shown in light gray and the indicated group is overlaid, colored by inferred pseudotime (top), group identity (middle) or local nuclear density (2D kernel density estimate, bottom). Young nuclei occupy a discrete low-pseudotime region, whereas AD nuclei are shifted toward high pseudotime. b, Group-specific kernel density estimates of pseudotime, with the pooled distribution shown in gray. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Dashed vertical lines mark mean pseudotime: young 1.50, CTL 2.38, AD 2.90 and AD_44 2.12. The distribution shifts rightward from young to CTL to AD. c, Empirical cumulative distributions of nuclear pseudotime. The maximal vertical separation between AD and CTL is the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance D = 0.27, presented as a descriptive effect size. Because nuclei within a donor are not independent, inference used donor-level mean pseudotime: AD versus CTL, 6 versus 7 donors, two-sided exact Wilcoxon rank-sum test, P = 0.0047. Young and AD_44 are shown descriptively and were not tested. d, Group composition of 22 fixed-width pseudotime bins (width 0.2, early to late from left to right). Each bar highlights the fraction of nuclei contributed by each group. Nucleus and donor counts are as in a. Young and AD_44 were shown descriptively and were not tested. The AD fraction increases along pseudotime (Spearman ρ = 0.97, n = 22 bins, two-sided unadjusted P = 1.0 × 10−13), from near-absence in the earliest bins to dominance in the latest bins. A donor-aware binomial mixed model (in-segment versus out, group + (1 | donor), two-sided Wald tests, BH-adjusted across 44 segment × comparison tests) showed AD nuclei were underrepresented relative to CTL in early bins 4–9 (log-OR − 3.23 to −1.28, adjusted P ≤ 0.017) and overrepresented in late bins 16–21 (log-OR +0.62 to +1.31, adjusted P ≤ 0.044), with a single crossover at pseudotime ≈ 2.3–2.9.   • Sources indicate that after losing two continental finals in the last two years, Atletico Mineiro will look to change that story this Saturday, November 21, against Boca Juniors in the Copa Sudamericana final at the Estadio Metropolitano Roberto Melendez in Barranquilla.
  • In a recent development, eduardo Dominguez’s side arrive winless in seven games and must rediscover the attacking output that underpinned their run through the tournament.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Saikat Mandal | 20 Nov 2026 10:33, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 10:33.

Sources indicate that after losing two continental finals in the last two years, Atletico Mineiro will look to change that story this Saturday, November 21, against Boca Juniors in the Copa Sudamericana final at the Estadio Metropolitano Roberto Melendez in Barranquilla. Atletico Mineiro are chasing their first title in the competition, while the Argentines are aiming for a third following triumphs in 2004 and 2005.

In a recent development, eduardo Dominguez’s side arrive winless in seven games and must rediscover the attacking output that underpinned their run through the tournament. Boca Juniors, under Rodolfo Arruabarrena, have won their last six matches, four of them without conceding, and head into the final in considerably better form, one that also carries a place in the 2027 Copa Libertadores group stage and the next Recopa Sudamericana.

Industry observers note that atletico Mineiro built their Copa Sudamericana campaign on six wins, two draws and four defeats, scoring 18 goals and conceding 14. Topping Group B secured a direct route into the last 16.

In the knockout rounds, Atletico Mineiro faced contrasting scenarios. They eliminated RB Bragantino 3-2 on aggregate, fought back in Belo Horizonte after losing the first leg to Santos, and confirmed their place on penalties following a dramatic tie.

The semi-final again highlighted that inconsistency. Atletico Mineiro built a 3-0 lead over Montevideo City Torque at the Arena MRV and, despite losing 2-0 in Uruguay, held on to progress thanks to the cushion from the first leg.

It has been revealed that the main concern is recent form. Since their last Brasileirao win, Atletico Mineiro have picked up five defeats and two draws, scored just three goals in that spell, and failed to find the net in five of those seven matches.

That slump adds to the emotional weight of the two continental finals Atletico Mineiro have already lost in recent seasons, to Botafogo in the 2024 Copa Libertadores and to Lanus in the 2025 Copa Sudamericana. In another final, how the squad handles that pressure could have a direct bearing on their performance.

Their continental record against Argentine opposition, however, offers a point of confidence. Atletico Mineiro have not lost in regulation time to a side from the country in 14 official matches, with nine wins and five draws, a record Dominguez is likely to draw on to lift his squad in the pursuit of the title.

Sources indicate that boca Juniors dropped into the Copa Sudamericana after finishing third in their Copa Libertadores group. Since then, they have rebuilt their campaign, winning five, drawing one and losing two in the knockout phase, scoring 13 goals and conceding just five.

Recent findings suggest that their run began with a penalty-shootout win over O’Higgins and gained momentum in the last 16, when they beat Recoleta home and away. In the quarter-finals, they managed the advantage built at home and eliminated Sao Paulo with a draw in Brazil.

In a recent development, the semi-final demanded a stronger response. Having been beaten by Vasco da Gama at La Bombonera, Boca Juniors turned the tie around at the Maracana, showing they could raise their level when needing a result away from home.

Recent form backs up that improvement. Boca Juniors have won six matches in a row across all competitions, scoring 11 goals and conceding just two, a run that combines sharper finishing with a more settled defence. They also arrive on the back of the Liga Argentina title, secured with a stoppage-time Enner Valencia goal in a win over Defensa y Justicia on November 7.

It has been revealed that against Brazilian sides in continental competition in 2026, Boca Juniors have two wins, two draws and two defeats, with six goals scored and five conceded. In the overall head-to-head, the Argentines hold the edge, but Atletico Mineiro have won the two most recent knockout meetings between the clubs, adding some balance to the final’s history.

Atletico Mineiro will be without Alan Franco for the final through suspension, with the midfielder also managing a left adductor injury. Maycon, Victor Hugo and Thiago Borbas are still waiting on medical clearance, while Reinier and Alan Minda are in a more delicate situation and are both expected to miss out.

Lyanco has returned to training but remains a doubt after missing the last two games. Fred, Ruan and Cassierra have already come back and featured against Mirassol, while Bernard remains one of the side’s main attacking outlets in the competition.

Industry observers note that at Boca Juniors, Agustin Marchesin is out with a knee ligament injury and was not even registered for the competition, although he has travelled with the squad. Lautaro Blanco and Milton Delgado have returned to training and are expected to start, with their physical progress still being monitored up to the final.

It has been revealed that rodrigo Battaglia has also returned to training with the group, widening Arruabarrena’s options. In attack, Tomas Aranda is competing with Alan Velasco and Leonel Flores, with no official word yet on who will complete the forward line alongside Sebastian Villa and Miguel Merentiel.

Atletico Mineiro possible starting lineup:.

In a recent development, everson; Natanael, Ruan, Vitao, Renan Lodi; Kevin Castano, Maycon, Fred; Tomas Cuello, Thiago Borbas, Bernard. Manager: Eduardo Dominguez.

Boca Juniors possible starting lineup:.

Alvaro Montero; Leandro Lozano, Lautaro Di Lollo, Facundo Herrera, Lautaro Blanco; Santiago Ascacibar, Leandro Paredes, Milton Delgado; Alan Velasco (Tomas Aranda), Sebastian Villa, Miguel Merentiel. Manager: Rodolfo Arruabarrena.

In a recent development, boca Juniors arrive in the more solid moment and have shown greater composure in controlling matches. If they can impose their rhythm, they stand to exploit the difficulties Atletico Mineiro have had reacting under pressure.

Atletico Mineiro still have the quality to cause problems, but the dip in form and the fitness doubts narrow their margin for error. The projection, therefore, is for a narrow Boca Juniors win, in a tight final likely to be decided by small details.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tottenham Hotspur will be disappointed if the FA decide against using their world-class stadium to host upcoming Nations League games.
  • That is according to former Manchester City financial adviser Stefan Borson, who exclusively told Football Insider that Premier League clubs are competing for extra revenue all the time.
  • With England now into the Nations League quarter-finals, the FA are considering a bid for the semi-final and final clashes later in the season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham Hotspur will be disappointed if the FA decide against using their world-class stadium to host upcoming Nations League games.

That is according to former Manchester City financial adviser Stefan Borson, who exclusively told Football Insider that Premier League clubs are competing for extra revenue all the time.

With England now into the Nations League quarter-finals, the FA are considering a bid for the semi-final and final clashes later in the season.

Thomas Tuchel's side will face Norway over two legs in March, with growing confidence that the Three Lions can reach the latter stages.

With Wembley occupied for these later games, the obvious destination would be the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, but the FA have different ideas.

It is understood that stadiums further north would be considered more heavily, with Everton's Hill Dickinson already in the conversation.

Ultimately, that will be a significant blow for Spurs, who would have seen a financial upside to hosting the games at their stadium.

Speaking exclusively to Football Insider, Borson explained: "They've got this venue that they'd like to rent out more frequently if they could.

Recent findings suggest that "The vast majority of the time, each of these stadiums all around the country, the vast majority of the year, they are empty. They've got the lights on the grass, and they're empty.

"So clearly if you can fill them more often, brilliant. I don't think it's much more complicated than that. That's what they're all trying to do, all competing to have more events at their stadium.

Industry observers note that "And the events that they have, they want to be as trouble-free as possible. Can you get a football match where you don't even need to move the pitch?

"And you're literally opening up the stadium, filling it with the same stewarding that you would do for a match for a normal match day?

Recent findings suggest that "People come in, you get your cut of the revenue, you get, effectively, your rental fee. You get some upside from product being sold. And they leave.

Industry observers note that "And that's it. It's like any venue; you'd like to rent it out. You'd like it to be full practically most nights.".

If you're a fan of the NFL, you'll be well aware of the relationship that Spurs have forged with American football supporters outside of the normal season.

While Borson believes that Spurs' profit from hosting these NFL matches is far more likely to be closer to £1million, it's still profit at the of the day.

It also brings upcoming people to the capital, helping the surrouding areas, while also making use of an incredible stadium when it wouldn't normally be in use.

Hosting Nations League games would simply be another feather in Spurs' cap, but it doesn't look like that's going to happen this season.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apollo Global Management were always going to scrap their €2billion (£1.5billion) loan after Manchester City's guilty verdict.

That is according to former Man City financial adviser Stefan Borson, who exclusively told Football Insider that Apollo were never going to get committee approval to proceed with their investment.

It has emerged that Apollo, a US private capital group, pulled out of an eye-watering loan to the Citizens' owners in the final stages of discussions.

This came after an independent commission found Man City guilty on 114 counts of finance-related breaches between 2009 and 2018.

The 10-time Premier League winners, of course, have claimed innocence and submitted an appeal, and fans should soon discover the result.

The Financial Times' latest enhancement has spread more uncertainty around Man City's case and the potential punishment, but the move hasn't "surprised" Borson in the slightest.

Speaking exclusively to Football Insider, Borson has explained the relationship between Man City's owners and Apollo, and why investment was never possible after the guilty verdict.

Recent findings suggest that "There are a couple of interesting things about the story. First of all, Apollo took a minority stake in Mubadala, which is the very large sovereign wealth investment fund out of Abu Dhabi," he remarked.

Industry observers note that "It's chaired by Manchester City's chairman, Khaldun Al Mubarak. And they have investments in a who's who of the best businesses in the world.

"They're really one of the most preeminent global investors with connections throughout the US, and they're co-investing with some of the best-known American funds.

"So the fact that Apollo and Mubadala have a relationship is not a surprise, and they doubled down on that with the investment that happened just before the release of the decision.

"But likewise, there's no realistic way in which any credit committee in an organization like Apollo which has underlying investors and pension funds and other institutional money, would get credit committee approval following the decision of the independent commission.".

Man City's sponsors, Etihad and Etisalat, have hit back at the independent commision's findings, labelling them "entirely false and defamatory".

And they may well be upset about being dragged into the situation, but can they really attempt to sue the Premier League board members individually.

The short answer? No. At least, Borson doesn't believe so, given that board members, especially Richard Masters, have only spoken facts so far.

Recent findings suggest that suing the Premier League as an entirety is completely different, and even that is unlikely to be successful. But the Premier League have come prepared with the latest vote.

Premier League clubs voted in favour of paying the Premier League board member's legal fees should Man City's sponsors push ahead with legal action.

Neymar branded Coritiba a 'small f****** team' in a rant at rival supporters who taunted him.

The Brazilian football icon screamed inside the tunnel as he was drawn into a heated exchange with Remo's directors.

Meanwhile, while he mocked Remo over being eliminated from the cup, Santos went out in the quarter-finals 3-0 on aggregate to Palmeiras.

Neymar has had a fairly effective season personally, scoring 10 goals and recording eight assists in all competitions while captaining Santos.

'We know that in every transfer window, offers come in for him to leave. Yet Neymar always chooses to stay at Santos. What I'm anticipating is that, first and foremost, I need to keep Neymar happy. Do you understand?' he mentioned.

According to recent reports, 'And if he's happy here, I can keep him here. So, look, down this final stretch, the work we've done to structure the squad and open up positive possibilities has given us the license to dream.'.

Neymar, who was widely regarded as one of the greatest footballers of his generation during his time at Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain, returned to his boyhood club Santos from Saudi Arabian club Al-Hilal in January 2025.

His £200million move from Barcelona to Paris Saint-Germain remains the most expensive transfer of all time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The prospect of taking over at Everton is likely to be hugely attractive for several American investment groups.

That is according to former Toffees chief executive Keith Wyness, speaking exclusively to Football Insider, who believes that European football clubs remain “very sought after” across the Atlantic.

This comes after recent reports suggested that the appetite among US investors for owning European clubs is slowly beginning to die off.

However, Wyness does not believe that is the case, and believes that there is still a strong market for clubs in Europe.

He previously told Football Insider that the USA is the most likely source for Everton’s next ownership group, with The Friedkins already looking to sell.

However, any takeover deal is unlikely to be completed until next summer, with the saga still in its early stages at the moment.

Everton’s former chief Wyness – who served as CEO at Goodison Park between 2004 and 2009 and now runs a football consultancy advising elite clubs – believes that Premier League clubs still have significant appeal for US investors, and Everton should have no issues finding a buyer.

The Merseysiders are already part of a group of 11 Premier League clubs to be owned by Americans, and are most likely to remain part of that group.

Speaking on the latest edition of Football Insider’s Inside Track podcast, Wyness explained that Everton won’t be concerned about a lack of interest.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t know where that’s coming from. In general, in the US, as you say, the US investor appetite for European clubs is good,” he mentioned.

It has been revealed that “I think there is a lot of interest still from American investors in general. So I'd have to argue with that one.

Recent findings suggest that “European football clubs in general are still very sought after, and sports clubs as an asset class are still very sought after. So, no, I don't see that being an issue, and as a result I think there'll be a good market, which is good news for Everton.”.

Former Everton scout Bryan King told Football Insider earlier this week that Everton winger Carlos Alcaraz and his agent are both unhappy with his level of game time right now.

The Argentine has played just 14 minutes of Premier League football so far this term, and has become something of a forgotten man at the Hill Dickinson Stadium.

Alcaraz is also out of contract next summer, and King believes that if Everton don’t have the offer of a new deal on the table before January, then his agent will push for an early exit.

The 23-year-old has hardly featured in David Moyes’ prepares across the last 12 months, and could now be heading towards the end of his time with the club.

Newcastle United suffered a painful, chastening defeat, comprehensively beaten by Coventry City in a performance that should send a shudder of fear through Tyneside.

It has been revealed that it was a dreadful night for the visitors, who conceded four goals for the second successive away game. The manner in which they fell apart was damning. Whatever the supposed style of play, it is not good to watch: long balls are pumped forward for short strikers to chase or compete for in the air against far taller centre-backs. Away from home, it is becoming ineffective.

Newcastle are too easy to create chances against and there is not much that gets you excited when they attack.

According to recent reports, matthias Jaissle’s side did create chances against Coventry, but are not clinical and do not inspire confidence they can be with the players they have. Defensively, they escaped earlier in the season, but are now being exposed and punished. “Not good enough in both boxes,” was Jaissle’s blunt verdict. “To concede eight goals in two away games is not good enough.”.

Matthias Jaissle on this evening's defeat at the Coventry Building Society Arena. https://t.co/216NW6Laz8.

Newcastle’s misery was in stark contrast to the joyous celebrations from Coventry. This was a thoroughly deserved first home win of the season for Frank Lampard’s side.

“It was an outstanding performance,” the manager said. “We knew we would have to suffer at times against a team like Newcastle. But we were really good at the basics, winning the second balls, winning the duels, those moments are critical. It’s not always about pretty patterns, it’s about work ethic.”.

According to recent reports, the win lifts Coventry level on points with Manchester United and will give them fresh confidence at this level. This could be the start of something special for them.
